title: World 2 · The Straight Line
text:
Briefing

m1 <- lm(sbp ~ salt_g, data = ncd)
round(coef(m1), 2)

(Intercept)      salt_g 
     107.42        3.39 



Slope in units. The slope is the difference in mean SBP (mmHg) per extra gram of daily salt, across people. The intercept is the mean at zero, often outside the data.


new_salt <- tibble(salt_g = c(5, 8, 12))
cbind(salt_g = new_salt$salt_g,
      fit = round(predict(m1, new_salt), 1),
      CI = apply(round(predict(m1, new_salt, interval = "confidence")[, 2:3], 0), 1, paste, collapse = "–"),
      PI = apply(round(predict(m1, new_salt, interval = "prediction")[, 2:3], 0), 1, paste, collapse = "–"))

  salt_g fit     CI        PI       
1 "5"    "124.4" "123–126" "95–154" 
2 "8"    "134.5" "133–136" "105–164"
3 "12"   "148.1" "145–151" "118–178"



CI vs PI. The confidence interval is about the mean of a group; the prediction interval is about one new person and includes the residual scatter, so it is far wider.


r2(m1)

# R2 for Linear Regression
       R2: 0.202
  adj. R2: 0.200



R² vs adjusted R². R² never falls when variables are added; adjusted R² charges a penalty per parameter. Centring (for example age at 50) makes the intercept the expected outcome at a meaningful value without changing the slope.

title: World 2 · The Straight Line
text:
Level 1 · Slope, prediction, residuals

A model gives sbp = 107.4 + 3.4 × salt_g. What does the 3.4 mean?

Daily salt accounts for 3.4 mmHg of each person’s own SBP
Mean SBP is 3.4 mmHg higher per extra gram of daily salt
Each extra gram of daily salt raises SBP by 3.4 percent
Each person’s SBP rises 3.4 mmHg whenever their daily salt rises 1 g



Using sbp = 107.4 + 3.4 × salt_g, what mean SBP (mmHg, nearest whole number) is predicted at 10 g/day?


A man eating 10 g/day has SBP 150 mmHg while the line predicts 141.4. What is his residual (observed − fitted)?

title: World 2 · The Straight Line
text:
Level 2 · Intervals and R²

At 8 g/day the 95% CI for mean SBP is 133–136 but the 95% prediction interval is 105–164. Why is the second so much wider?

Prediction intervals are built from the sample range directly
It adds person-to-person scatter to the uncertainty of the line
Prediction intervals are computed at a higher confidence level than 95%
The line is less precisely estimated at 8 g than at 10 g



r2(lm(sbp ~ salt_g))           # R2: 0.202   adj. R2: 0.200
r2(lm(sbp ~ salt_g + z1:z20))  # R2: 0.227   adj. R2: 0.198
z1:z20 are twenty random-noise columns. What should you conclude?

Adjusted R² must exceed R², so one of the lines is wrong
An R² near 0.2 means the salt model is of no use
The twenty extra variables clearly helped because R² rose by 0.025
The noise columns did not help: adjusted R² did not improve

title: World 2 · The Straight Line
text:
Level 3 · Centring

Age spans 30–69 years and the intercept of sbp ~ age is 96 mmHg, which describes nobody. What makes it interpretable?

Standardise SBP so that its mean becomes zero
Centre age at 50 so the intercept is expected SBP at 50
Delete everyone younger than 30 from the dataset
Multiply age by 100 so that the slope looks much bigger



Put the steps for a centred model in order, from first to last:

Choose a meaningful reference value such as age 50
Read the intercept as the mean outcome at the reference value
Refit the model using the centred variable
Create the centred variable by subtracting that value
Confirm that the slope did not change

title: World 2 · The Straight Line
text:
Boss · Interpretation inspector

Boss: flag every flawed sentence about sbp = 107 + 3.4 × salt_g (R² = 0.20, n = 582, cross-sectional survey).

Each extra gram of daily salt goes with 3.4 mmHg higher mean SBP.
The model accounts for about 20% of the variability in SBP.
An adult eating 0 g of salt would have an SBP of exactly 107 mmHg.
Adding 5 g of salt to one patient’s diet will raise that patient’s SBP by 17 mmHg.
The 95% prediction interval at 8 g/day is narrower than the 95% CI for the mean.
Because R² is only 0.20, the salt association is clinically unimportant.

title: Dungeons & Dataframes — Site design
text:
Dungeons & Dataframes is a website for learning medical statistics in R, for community-medicine residents and faculty who already have basic-to-moderate R. It is organised into tracks (Track 1 = Regression, others planned: comparing groups, epidemiological measures, study design and sample size, surveys, evidence synthesis, reporting). It is not a course with a game bolted on; it is a place you play in: a map of worlds, a skill tree that shows what you can and cannot do yet, case files that feel like real thesis problems, an arcade for quick drills, and a lab bench where you run real R.







Design goal
How the site delivers it




Mastery, not completion
Progress is measured per skill (≈ 70 nodes), with spaced review. Worlds are story containers.


Varied retrieval
Every skill is practised in three modes (Quest, Case file, Arcade) so it is learned, not memorised.


Judgement over recall
Items ask what a result means, what to do, or compute something. Never function recall (enforced by lint_bank.R).


Real R, real data
Hybrid R labs on the project datasets, verified by result codes (no server).


Works anywhere
Static site, offline-capable, local progress; accounts and dashboards can be added later without a rewrite.


Kind to learners
A calm mode removes streaks, toasts and ranks; hints are cheap; nothing locks permanently.



Audience assumption: can import data, use dplyr/ggplot2 basics, and run and print a model. A readiness check advises anyone who is not there yet (Roadmap §2.3).

2. Information architecture
Dungeons & Dataframes
├── 🏠 Campus (home)            today's plan, streak, daily review, continue, news
├── 🌳 Skill tree               ~70 skills in 16 branches; mastery levels; "what next?"
├── 🧭 Tracks                   Regression (live) · Comparing groups · Epi measures · …

title: Dungeons & Dataframes — Site design
text:
6. The hybrid R lab bench
Principle: learners practise in their own R with the real packages; the site verifies via short result codes: no server, works offline, and codes are not transferable.

6.1 Flow

Open the world’s lab (the existing fill-in-the-blank scripts, regenerated from solutions with build_labs.R).
source("rqlab.R") (or library(rqlab)) → rq_start(seed = "dr-a-2026"). The seed regenerates the dataset (or a subsample) so numbers differ per learner.
After each task: rq_check("task-3", m_adj) gives instant local feedback (“right outcome, wrong predictor”) and costs nothing.
At the end: rq_submit() prints a result code, e.g. RQ3-7F2K-91XA-Q0MD: a hash of (lab id, lab version, seed, per-task results).
Paste the code into the site’s Lab bench page; the page recomputes the hash from the task results encoded in the code’s payload and awards XP + skill credit.



6.2 What is checked
Object exists and has the right class/formula; estimates within tolerance (relative 1%); required output produced; for write-up tasks a self-check rubric (checklist) instead of auto-grading.


6.3 Strengths and limits

✔ No server; real R; instant feedback; per-learner numbers.
✔ Same grader runs in CI against the solution (must pass) and the blank lab (must fail).
✖ A determined learner can forge a code (it is a hash, not a signature). Acceptable for self-learning; credentialed attempts use server-side verification in the accounts phase.
Optional later: webR mode (R in the browser) after a package-compatibility spike; same checks, no copy-paste.

title: Dungeons & Dataframes — Site design
section: 8. State and data design (static now, accounts later)
text:
8. State and data design (static now, accounts later)

8.1 Principles

Events are truth, totals are derived. Store an append-only event log (attempt, hint, show-answer, review result, lab submitted, test submitted); recompute XP, mastery, rank and badges from it. This makes sync and re-balancing safe.
Storage adapter interface { load(), append(events), snapshot(), sync?() } with a LocalAdapter today; RemoteAdapter later (same interface).
Versioned schema + migrations (v: 2 …); import validates and migrates.
Idempotent items: an item pays XP once; replays are recorded but pay 0.
Pseudonymous IDs; no personal health data from learners.



8.2 Schema v2 (sketch)
{
  "v": 2, "learner": {"id": "uuid", "seed": "dr-a-2026", "created": "2026-10-14"},
  "settings": {"calm": false, "theme": "light", "reducedMotion": false, "textSize": 1},
  "events": [ {"t": 1760400000, "type": "attempt", "item": "w3-04", "mode": "quest", "ok": true, "hints": 1, "tries": 1},
              {"t": …, "type": "review", "skill": "A5", "ok": true},
              {"t": …, "type": "lab", "lab": "lab3", "code": "RQ3-…", "tasks": {"t1": true}},
              {"t": …, "type": "test", "kind": "pre", "score": 6, "total": 12, "byTag": {…}, "conf": {…}} ],
  "derived": {"xp": 640, "rank": "Epidemiologist", "badges": {…}, "skills": {"A5": {"level": 3, "box": 2, "due": "2026-10-21"}}}
}
derived is a cache that can always be rebuilt from events.


8.3 Accounts later: what changes (and what does not)

Unchanged: content, engine logic, item markup, skills.json, event schema.
Added: RemoteAdapter (sign-in via magic link/SSO), server endpoints for event append and snapshot, conflict policy (union of events by (t, id); derived recomputed), instructor read-only views, server-side lab/code verification, consent and data-deletion endpoints (DPDP Act 2023).

title: Dungeons & Dataframes — Site design
text:
10. Technology

Stay static and vanilla: Quarto pages + modular ES modules (engine/, modes/, ui/) bundled without a framework; no runtime dependencies; offline-first; optional PWA.
Refactor quest.js into modules in Phase 2: state (events, derive), items (renderers), modes (quest, casefile, arcade, review), skills (graph, recommender), adapters (local, remote), ui (HUD, toasts, tree).
Skill-tree rendering: inline SVG generated from skills.json (no library), keyboard navigable.
Arcade generators: plots pre-generated as SVG/PNG variants at build time (R) for the first release; client-side generation later for numeric games.
Accessibility: WCAG 2.2 AA; all interactions keyboard operable; no colour-only cues; reduced-motion honoured; screen-reader labels for tree nodes and drag-like items (button alternatives exist).
Performance budget: < 150 KB JS, < 60 KB CSS per page; pages usable on low-end phones.
English only: strings kept in one place for maintainability; no translation planned.

title: Dungeons & Dataframes — Site design
text:
11. Look, feel and voice

A friendly guide character (“Dr. Beta”) gives hints and debriefs: short, kind, never sarcastic about mistakes.
Visual style: clean field-medicine palette (navy/teal/amber), generous spacing, large touch targets, one accent for “correct”, one for “try again” (never red-only).
Microcopy: feedback explains why (“The OR is 5.1 but 50% of the exposed group have the outcome, so …”) before saying do this.
Calm mode: no streaks, ranks, toasts or timers; XP hidden; mastery shown as plain checkmarks.

text:
13. Open questions

Name Decided: Dungeons & Dataframes (D&D pun; tagline: medical statistics in R, one dungeon at a time). Not checked for trademark/domain availability.
Language scope Decided: English only.
Who reviews statistics Decided: the author (community-medicine faculty); optional external statistician check before wide release.
Pilot cohort: which residents/department, and when can a first cohort test Worlds 1–2 and the pre/post forms?
Credentialing Decided: completion certificate is a later priority (needs accounts and server verification; Phase 6).

title: Pre-test · Baseline check
text:
This baseline is not graded. Answer from what you know; rate your confidence honestly. Your skill breakdown shows which worlds to prioritise, and your post-test later shows your gain. Order of options is shuffled every time.



The number of dengue cases reported per ward per month is the outcome. Which family is the natural starting point?

Poisson or negative binomial regression
Cox proportional hazards regression for survival
Multinomial logistic regression
Ordinal logistic regression for ordered categories



In a model for systolic BP, BMI has β = 0.9. Which statement is correct?

Mean SBP is 0.9 mmHg higher per extra BMI unit, others fixed
Each person’s SBP rises 0.9 mmHg if their BMI rises 1
SBP is 0.9 percent higher for each extra BMI unit in the sample
BMI explains 0.9 of the variance in blood pressure



The residual SD is 12 mmHg. About how many mmHg is the half-width of a 95% prediction interval for one new patient? (whole number)


Adding ten pure-noise variables to a regression will usually…

lower R² because noise adds extra error
leave R² unchanged but widen the confidence intervals
raise R² a little but leave adjusted R² flat or lower
raise both R² and adjusted R² by a clearly visible margin



BMI is centred at 25 kg/m² before fitting. The intercept now represents…

the expected outcome for a person with BMI 25
the average outcome across all participants
the expected outcome at a BMI of zero
the change in the outcome for each extra unit of BMI



The crude β of salt on SBP is 5.0; adjusted for age it is 2.0. The most sensible reading is that…

age confounds the association and explains much of the slope
the adjusted model contains a calculation error somewhere in it
salt has no real effect once age is included in the model
age is a mediator, so adjusting for it is a mistake



With urban as the reference, rural = +4.0 and semi-urban = +1.5 mmHg. How many mmHg higher is rural than semi-urban? (1 decimal)


A thesis reports the final model of backward stepwise selection with no other justification. The main objection is that…

AIC cannot be computed for linear regression models
backward selection can only ever add new variables to the model
stepwise selection forbids adjusting for any confounder
p-values and CIs ignore the search and look too optimistic



Patients are drawn from 8 hospitals and share unmeasured hospital effects. Which assumption is most at risk?

Absence of influential points
Linearity of the age effect
Independence of observations
Normality of the outcome variable



Disease prevalence is 20%. What are the odds of disease? (2 decimals)


The adjusted OR for smoking is 0.60 (95% CI 0.45–0.80). Which wording is correct?

Smokers had 40% lower odds of the outcome, adjusted
Smokers were 40% less likely to have the outcome
The OR is below 1, so the result is not significant
Smoking prevents 40% of cases in this population



Flag every flawed sentence from this results paragraph (cross-sectional study, 32% prevalence).

Men had 2.1 times the odds of hypertension (95% CI 1.3–3.5).
Therefore men were 2.1 times as likely to be hypertensive.
Each year of age was associated with 0.6 mmHg higher SBP (95% CI 0.5–0.7).
The model explains 29% of the variance in hypertension (Tjur R² = 0.29).
Salt was kept because backward stepwise selection retained it.
BMI had β = 0.88.

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
Where we are

Sessions 2–4: continuous outcome → linear regression
Today: binary outcome (hypertension yes/no) → logistic regression
By the end you can:

explain odds, log-odds and why we exponentiate β into an OR
build crude and adjusted ORs with CIs
compare models by likelihood ratio test and AIC; read pseudo-R² honestly
judge calibration and discrimination (Hosmer–Lemeshow, ROC/AUC)
know when the OR overstates the prevalence ratio

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
Hypertension in our survey

ncd |> count(htn_f) |> mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  htn_f      n percent
  <fct>  <int>   <dbl>
1 No HTN   408      68
2 HTN      192      32



32% of adults are hypertensive — a common outcome. (Remember this for the OR vs PR discussion.)

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: Why not just use linear regression?
text:
Why not just use linear regression?

lpm <- lm(htn ~ age + salt_g + bmi + sex, data = cc)     # "linear probability model"
range(fitted(lpm))

[1] -0.3403238  0.9396895

sum(fitted(lpm) < 0)                                      # people with a negative "probability"

[1] 50




Fit a straight line to a 0/1 outcome and some people get a negative “probability”.

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: A straight line leaves the 0–1 range
text: A straight line leaves the 0–1 range

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: Three problems with a straight line for a 0/1 outcome
text:
Three problems with a straight line for a 0/1 outcome







Problem
Why




Impossible predictions
A line is unbounded: probabilities fall below 0 or above 1


Non-constant variance
The variance of a 0/1 outcome is p(1 − p): it depends on the mean


Non-normal errors
Residuals can only take two values per fitted value





Idea: model a transformation of the probability that can take any value from −∞ to +∞ — the log-odds.

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: Three ways to express the same risk
text:
Three ways to express the same risk

odds = p ÷ (1 − p)
log-odds = ln(odds) = ln [ p ÷ (1 − p) ]


tibble(probability = c(.10, .25, .32, .50, .75, .90)) |>
  mutate(odds = round(probability / (1 - probability), 2),
         `log-odds` = round(log(odds), 2))

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  probability  odds `log-odds`
        <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>
1        0.1   0.11      -2.21
2        0.25  0.33      -1.11
3        0.32  0.47      -0.76
4        0.5   1          0   
5        0.75  3          1.1 
6        0.9   9          2.2 



Worked example: our prevalence is 32% → odds = 0.32 ÷ 0.68 = 0.47 (“about 1 hypertensive for every 2 non-hypertensive”) → log-odds = ln 0.47 = −0.75.

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: The logit scale is unbounded and symmetric
text: The logit scale is unbounded and symmetric

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
A 2×2 example: age and hypertension

tab <- ncd |> count(age50, htn_f) |> pivot_wider(names_from = htn_f, values_from = n)
tab <- tab |> mutate(risk = round(HTN / (HTN + `No HTN`), 3), odds = round(HTN / `No HTN`, 3))
tab

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  age50 `No HTN`   HTN  risk  odds
  <fct>    <int> <int> <dbl> <dbl>
1 <50 y      265    51 0.161 0.192
2 50+ y      143   141 0.496 0.986

c(OR = tab$odds[2] / tab$odds[1], PR = tab$risk[2] / tab$risk[1]) |> round(2)

  OR   PR 
5.14 3.08 



Among 50+ the odds are 0.986, among <50 0.192: OR = 5.1. The prevalence ratio is only 3.1. Keep this gap in mind.

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
The logistic regression equation

logit(p) = ln [ p ÷ (1 − p) ] = β0 + β1x1 + β2x2 + …


The right side is just like linear regression
The left side is the log-odds of the outcome
Solve for the probability: p = 1 ÷ (1 + exp[ −(β0 + β1x1 + …) ]) — always between 0 and 1
Coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood, not least squares

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
Fitting it: glm(family = binomial)

m_crude <- glm(htn ~ salt_g, data = cc, family = binomial)
summary(m_crude)$coefficients |> round(3)

            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)   -3.648      0.400  -9.110        0
salt_g         0.376      0.049   7.665        0



β for salt = 0.38 — a change in log-odds per g/day. Not yet something a clinician can use: next we convert it.

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
The S-shaped curve

ggplot(cc, aes(salt_g, htn)) +
  geom_jitter(height = .03, alpha = .25, colour = col_blue) +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = binomial), colour = col_red, formula = y ~ x) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Salt intake (g/day)", y = "Probability of hypertension")

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: Step 1 — the model speaks in log-odds
text:
Step 1 — the model speaks in log-odds

ln [ odds(x) ] = β0 + β1 x

β1 is the change in log-odds for a one-unit increase in x. We want a ratio of odds, so compare the model at x + 1 and at x.

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
Step 2 — compare x + 1 with x

ln [ odds(x + 1) ] = β0 + β1 (x + 1) = β0 + β1x + β1



ln [ odds(x + 1) ] − ln [ odds(x) ] = (β0 + β1x + β1) − (β0 + β1x) = β1




ln [ odds(x + 1) ÷ odds(x) ] = β1




OR = odds(x + 1) ÷ odds(x) = eβ1



The β0 and the x terms cancel: that is why the OR for a one-unit change does not depend on the starting value of x, nor on the other covariates (they cancel as well). A difference in logs is the log of a ratio; exponentiate both sides to undo the log.

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: Step 3 — a worked number from our model
text:
Step 3 — a worked number from our model

b_salt <- coef(m_adj)[["salt_g"]]
c(beta = b_salt, OR_per_1g = exp(b_salt), OR_per_5g = exp(5 * b_salt), same_as = exp(b_salt)^5) |> round(3)

     beta OR_per_1g OR_per_5g   same_as 
    0.214     1.238     2.914     2.914 



β = 0.214 → OR per g/day = e^0.214 = 1.24
Per 5 g/day: e^(5 × β) = 2.91 — ORs multiply, they do not add
“Each extra 1 g/day multiplies the odds of hypertension by 1.24, holding the other variables constant”

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: Check it directly with two different people
text:
Check it directly with two different people

profile <- tibble(age = c(35, 35, 62, 62), sex = factor(c("Female", "Female", "Male", "Male"), levels(cc$sex)),
                  salt_g = c(8, 9, 8, 9), bmi = c(22, 22, 29, 29),
                  residence = factor("Rural", levels(cc$residence)), education = factor("Primary", levels(cc$education)),
                  tobacco = factor("No", levels(cc$tobacco)), alcohol = factor("No", levels(cc$alcohol)),
                  phys_act = factor("low", levels(cc$phys_act)))
p <- predict(m_adj, profile, type = "response"); odds <- p / (1 - p)
c(young_woman = odds[2] / odds[1], older_man = odds[4] / odds[3]) |> round(3)

young_woman.2   older_man.4 
        1.238         1.238 



Whatever the person’s other characteristics, 8 → 9 g/day multiplies the odds by exactly e^β = 1.238. The probability change differs by person; the OR does not.

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: Confidence intervals: exponentiate the limits too
text:
Confidence intervals: exponentiate the limits too

ci_log <- confint(m_adj)["salt_g", ]                       # profile-likelihood CI on the log-odds scale
rbind(`log-odds (β)` = c(est = b_salt, ci_log), `odds ratio` = exp(c(est = b_salt, ci_log))) |> round(3)

               est 2.5 % 97.5 %
log-odds (β) 0.214 0.101  0.330
odds ratio   1.238 1.107  1.391



CI for β is built on the log scale, where it is (approximately) symmetric
Exponentiating each limit gives the CI for the OR: 1.24 (1.11 to 1.39)
Because exp stretches the right side more, the OR CI is asymmetric around the estimate

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: Symmetric on the β scale, asymmetric on the OR scale
text:
Symmetric on the β scale, asymmetric on the OR scale

bind_rows(
  tidy(m_adj, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = .95) |> mutate(scale = "log-odds (β)"),
  tidy(m_adj, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |> mutate(scale = "odds ratio (OR)")) |>
  filter(term %in% c("sexMale", "alcoholYes", "salt_g")) |>
  mutate(scale = fct_inorder(scale), null = if_else(scale == "odds ratio (OR)", 1, 0)) |>
  ggplot(aes(estimate, term)) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = null), linetype = "dashed", colour = col_red) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), colour = col_navy) +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = "Dashed line = no effect: β = 0 on the left, OR = 1 on the right")

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: Symmetric on the β scale, asymmetric on the OR scale
text: Symmetric on the β scale, asymmetric on the OR scale

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
Why OR = 1 corresponds to β = 0

e0 = 1 ⇒ β = 0 ⇔ OR = 1


OR = 1 means no change in the odds — no association
A CI for the OR that includes 1 is the same as a CI for β that includes 0 → not significant at 5%
OR > 1 = higher odds; OR < 1 = lower odds (β > 0 / β < 0)

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
Crude vs adjusted ORs

t_crude <- cc |> select(htn, salt_g, age, bmi, sex, residence, education, tobacco, alcohol, phys_act) |>
  tbl_uvregression(method = glm, y = htn, method.args = list(family = binomial), exponentiate = TRUE)
t_adj <- tbl_regression(m_adj, exponentiate = TRUE)
tbl_merge(list(t_crude, t_adj), tab_spanner = c("**Crude**", "**Adjusted**"))



Compare crude and adjusted: salt 1.46 → 1.24; education gradient disappears; physical activity appears only after adjustment (high activity OR about 0.57) — a first warning against screening variables by crude p-value (Session 6).

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: Reading an OR, its CI and its p-value
text:
Reading an OR, its CI and its p-value



Salt: adjusted OR 1.24 (95% CI 1.11–1.39), p < 0.001


Direction: OR > 1 → higher odds with more salt
Size: 24% higher odds per g/day; ≈ 3× per 5 g/day
Precision: CI excludes 1



Sex: adjusted OR 2.1 for men vs women (reference)


An OR is a ratio of odds, not a ratio of risks. For a common outcome, “twice the odds” is not “twice as likely” (see later).

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: Likelihood: how probable were the data we saw?
text:
Likelihood: how probable were the data we saw?

p_hat <- c(0.8, 0.3, 0.2)       # model's predicted P(hypertension) for 3 people
y     <- c(1,   0,   0)         # what actually happened
per_person <- ifelse(y == 1, p_hat, 1 - p_hat)
per_person

[1] 0.8 0.7 0.8

c(likelihood = prod(per_person), log_likelihood = sum(log(per_person)), deviance = -2 * sum(log(per_person))) |> round(3)

    likelihood log_likelihood       deviance 
         0.448         -0.803          1.606 



Likelihood = product of the probabilities the model gave to what really happened
Log-likelihood = its logarithm (easier arithmetic; always ≤ 0; closer to 0 = better fit)
Deviance = −2 × log-likelihood (relative to a perfect model): smaller = better fit

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: Maximum likelihood: the peak of the curve
text:
Maximum likelihood: the peak of the curve

bhat <- coef(m_crude)[["salt_g"]]
prof <- tibble(b = seq(bhat - .3, bhat + .3, length.out = 100)) |>
  mutate(ll = map_dbl(b, \(b) as.numeric(logLik(glm(htn ~ 1 + offset(b * salt_g), data = cc, family = binomial)))))
ci <- confint(m_crude)["salt_g", ]

ggplot(prof, aes(b, ll)) +
  geom_line(colour = col_navy, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = max(prof$ll) - qchisq(.95, 1) / 2, linetype = "dashed", colour = col_red) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(bhat, ci), linetype = c("solid", "dotted", "dotted"), colour = col_blue) +
  labs(x = "candidate β for salt (log-odds per g/day)", y = "log-likelihood",
       caption = "Peak = maximum-likelihood estimate · red line = 1.92 below the peak → the 95% CI")



Each point on the curve is the log-likelihood if the true salt β were that value (intercept re-optimised). The estimate sits at the peak. Values whose log-likelihood is within 1.92 of the peak (half of the chi-square 3.84 cut-off) form the likelihood-based 95% CI — this is what confint() uses.

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: Maximum likelihood: the peak of the curve
text: Maximum likelihood: the peak of the curve

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
Deviance and log-likelihood in R

tibble(model = c("intercept only", "salt only", "adjusted"),
       logLik   = c(logLik(glm(htn ~ 1, binomial, cc)), logLik(m_crude), logLik(m_adj)),
       deviance = c(deviance(glm(htn ~ 1, binomial, cc)), deviance(m_crude), deviance(m_adj)),
       params   = c(1, 2, length(coef(m_adj)))) |> mutate(across(c(logLik, deviance), ~ round(.x, 1)))

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  model          logLik deviance params
  <chr>           <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>
1 intercept only  -344.     687.      1
2 salt only       -308.     617.      2
3 adjusted        -256.     511.     13



More predictors → higher log-likelihood and lower deviance. The question is whether the improvement is more than chance — that is the likelihood ratio test.

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: Likelihood ratio test (LRT) for nested models
text:
Likelihood ratio test (LRT) for nested models

H₀: the extra coefficients are all zero. Test statistic = 2 × (logLikbig − logLiksmall) ~ χ² with df = number of extra parameters.


m_small <- glm(htn ~ age + sex, data = cc, family = binomial)
m_big   <- glm(htn ~ age + sex + salt_g + bmi + tobacco + alcohol + phys_act, data = cc, family = binomial)
anova(m_small, m_big, test = "LRT")

Analysis of Deviance Table

Model 1: htn ~ age + sex
Model 2: htn ~ age + sex + salt_g + bmi + tobacco + alcohol + phys_act
  Resid. Df Resid. Dev Df Deviance  Pr(>Chi)    
1       548     568.32                          
2       542     511.75  6   56.574 2.228e-10 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

lmtest::lrtest(m_small, m_big)

Likelihood ratio test

Model 1: htn ~ age + sex
Model 2: htn ~ age + sex + salt_g + bmi + tobacco + alcohol + phys_act
  #Df  LogLik Df  Chisq Pr(>Chisq)    
1   3 -284.16                         
2   9 -255.87  6 56.574  2.228e-10 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: Why LRT rather than Wald for comparing models
text:
Why LRT rather than Wald for comparing models



Multi-df terms: education has 3 dummies — Wald gives 3 separate p-values; the LRT asks “does education matter at all?” once
Small samples / big effects: Wald can be unreliable (Hauck–Donner)
LRT is invariant to re-parameterisation; Wald is not



drop1(m_adj, test = "LRT") |> as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("term") |> select(term, Df, AIC, LRT, `Pr(>Chi)`) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 3)))

        term Df AIC    LRT Pr(>Chi)
1     <none> NA 537     NA       NA
2     salt_g  1 549 14.100 1.70e-04
3        age  1 604 68.800 1.07e-16
4        bmi  1 549 13.900 1.95e-04
5        sex  1 545  9.380 2.19e-03
6  residence  1 535  0.149 7.00e-01
7  education  3 531  0.166 9.83e-01
8    tobacco  1 537  1.360 2.43e-01
9    alcohol  1 541  5.200 2.26e-02
10  phys_act  2 538  4.210 1.22e-01




drop1 refits the model without each term: one LRT per term including the 3-df education and 2-df physical activity terms.

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: AIC: comparing models that are not nested
text:
AIC: comparing models that are not nested

m_bmi   <- glm(htn ~ age + sex + bmi,   data = cc, family = binomial)
m_waist <- glm(htn ~ age + sex + waist, data = cc, family = binomial)
AIC(m_bmi, m_waist)

        df      AIC
m_bmi    4 549.4734
m_waist  4 548.3553



AIC = −2 log-likelihood + 2 × (number of parameters) — fit, penalised for complexity
Lower is better; a difference < 2 means essentially no preference
Works for non-nested comparisons (BMI vs waist) where an LRT cannot
Always compare on the same rows (watch missing data!)

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
Three pseudo-R² measures

r2(m_adj)                       # for logistic models r2() reports Tjur's R2

# R2 for Logistic Regression
  Tjur's R2: 0.292

tibble(measure = c("McFadden", "Nagelkerke", "Tjur"),
       value   = c(r2_mcfadden(m_adj)$R2[[1]], r2_nagelkerke(m_adj)[[1]], r2_tjur(m_adj)[[1]])) |>
  mutate(value = round(value, 2))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  measure    value
  <chr>      <dbl>
1 McFadden    0.26
2 Nagelkerke  0.38
3 Tjur        0.29



Three different numbers for one model — because they are different things.

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: How to use (and not use) pseudo-R²
text:
How to use (and not use) pseudo-R²



Not

the same as linear R²
“% of variance explained”
comparable across datasets or with R² from lm()




Do

remember their values run low (a McFadden of 0.2–0.4 is already a very good fit)
report one descriptively, naming it
compare models with LRT / AIC instead

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
Tjur’s R² has a picture


Tjur’s R² ≈ the gap between the mean predicted probability in people with and without the outcome. Handy — but still only descriptive.

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
Two different questions



Calibration
If the model says “30% risk”, do about 30% of such people actually have hypertension?



Discrimination
Does the model give higher predicted risk to people who have hypertension than to those who do not?

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
Calibration plot: predicted vs observed

cal <- cc |> mutate(p_hat = fitted(m_adj), decile = ntile(p_hat, 10)) |>
  group_by(decile) |> summarise(predicted = mean(p_hat), observed = mean(htn), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(cal, aes(predicted, observed)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = col_red) +
  geom_line(colour = col_navy) + geom_point(size = 3, colour = col_navy) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Mean predicted risk (decile of risk)", y = "Observed proportion with hypertension")

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text: Calibration plot: predicted vs observed

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
Hosmer–Lemeshow test

performance_hosmer(m_adj, n_bins = 10)

# Hosmer-Lemeshow Goodness-of-Fit Test

  Chi-squared: 12.051
           df:  8    
      p-value:  0.149





p > 0.05 → no evidence of poor calibration



Limitations: depends on the number of bins; low power in small samples, over-sensitive in huge ones; a single p-value does not show where the model fails. Prefer the calibration plot.

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
ROC curve and AUC

cc$p_hat <- fitted(m_adj)
roc_obj  <- roc(cc$htn, cc$p_hat, quiet = TRUE)

ggroc(roc_obj, colour = col_red, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 1, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = .45, y = .25, size = 6, hjust = 0,
           label = paste0("AUC = ", round(auc(roc_obj), 2))) +
  labs(x = "Specificity", y = "Sensitivity")

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text: ROC curve and AUC

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
Interpreting the AUC

auc(roc_obj)

Area under the curve: 0.8244

ci.auc(roc_obj)

95% CI: 0.7891-0.8597 (DeLong)



AUC = probability that a randomly chosen hypertensive gets a higher predicted risk than a randomly chosen normotensive
0.5 = coin toss · 0.7–0.8 acceptable · 0.8–0.9 good · > 0.9 excellent
Ours: 0.82 (95% CI 0.79–0.86)

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
A cut-off, and a caution

coords(roc_obj, "best", ret = c("threshold", "sensitivity", "specificity"), best.method = "youden") |> round(2)

  threshold sensitivity specificity
1      0.35        0.71        0.79



The “best” threshold depends on purpose: screening (favour sensitivity) vs confirmation (favour specificity)
AUC from the same data that fitted the model is optimistic — validate (new sample, cross-validation, bootstrap)
Good discrimination does not guarantee good calibration, and vice-versa

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: The OR overstates the PR when the outcome is common
text:
The OR overstates the PR when the outcome is common

risk <- tab$risk; or <- (risk[2] / (1 - risk[2])) / (risk[1] / (1 - risk[1])); pr <- risk[2] / risk[1]
c(prevalence_50plus = risk[2], prevalence_under50 = risk[1], PR = pr, OR = or) |> round(2)

 prevalence_50plus prevalence_under50                 PR                 OR 
              0.50               0.16               3.08               5.13 




“50+ year-olds have 5.1 times the odds” is true — but “5.1 times as likely” is wrong. They are 3.1 times as likely.

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: Why: the gap grows with baseline risk
text:
Why: the gap grows with baseline risk


OR ≈ PR only when the outcome is rare (< ~10%). With ~32% prevalence, the OR is far from the PR.

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
section: Getting a prevalence ratio: Poisson with robust SE
text:
Getting a prevalence ratio: Poisson with robust SE

m_pr <- glm(htn ~ age50, data = ncd, family = poisson)
m_or <- glm(htn ~ age50, data = ncd, family = binomial)
robust_vcov <- sandwich::vcovHC(m_pr, type = "HC0")

tibble(measure  = c("OR (logistic)", "PR (Poisson, robust SE)"),
       estimate = exp(c(coef(m_or)[[2]], coef(m_pr)[[2]])),
       lower    = exp(c(confint.default(m_or)[2, 1], coefci(m_pr, vcov. = robust_vcov)[2, 1])),
       upper    = exp(c(confint.default(m_or)[2, 2], coefci(m_pr, vcov. = robust_vcov)[2, 2]))) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2)))

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  measure                 estimate lower upper
  <chr>                      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 OR (logistic)               5.12  3.51  7.49
2 PR (Poisson, robust SE)     3.08  2.33  4.06



Poisson with robust (sandwich) SE gives a valid PR for a binary outcome
Log-binomial (glm(family = binomial(link = "log"))) gives the PR directly but can fail to converge — try it, fall back to Poisson-robust
Adjusted PRs work the same way (add covariates)

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
Self-check quiz (1/6)

Why is ordinary linear regression a poor choice for a 0/1 outcome?

It cannot include more than one predictor at a time
Predicted probabilities can leave the 0–1 range
It requires a much larger sample than other models
It only accepts categorical predictor variables

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
Self-check quiz (2/6)

In a logistic model β = 0.21 for salt, so e^β = 1.24. Which interpretation is correct?

Each extra g/day raises the probability of hypertension by 24 percentage points
Each extra g/day multiplies the odds of hypertension by 1.24, others constant
24% of all hypertension in the community is attributable to salt intake
People eating more salt are 1.24 times as likely to be hypertensive

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
Self-check quiz (3/6)

Which statement about pseudo-R² (McFadden, Nagelkerke, Tjur) is TRUE?

It gives the percentage of outcome variance the model explains
All three measures return the same value for a given model
It is a descriptive index, not read like linear R-squared
A value below 0.5 shows that the model is of no use

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression
text:
Self-check quiz (4/6)

Hypertension prevalence is 16% under 50 and 50% at 50+ (OR ≈ 5.1, PR ≈ 3.1). Which statement is best?

People aged 50+ are about 5 times as likely to be hypertensive
People aged 50+ are about 3 times as likely; the OR overstates here
The OR and the PR are identical whenever prevalence is above 10%
The prevalence ratio can only be calculated when the disease is rare

title: Session 5 — Logistic Regression

A logistic model gives β = 0.69 for a binary exposure. What odds ratio is this? (nearest 0.1)

Score and take-home
Your score: 

Logistic regression models the log-odds; e^β = odds ratio, CI limits exponentiated; OR = 1 ⇔ β = 0
Likelihood drives assessment: compare nested models by LRT, others by AIC
Pseudo-R² is descriptive, not “variance explained”
Calibration (plot > Hosmer–Lemeshow) and discrimination (AUC) answer different questions

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
section: Is the slope different from zero?
text:
Is the slope different from zero?

H₀: β = 0 (no linear association) H₁: β ≠ 0


tidy(m_crude, conf.int = TRUE) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 3)))

# A tibble: 2 × 7
  term        estimate std.error statistic   p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)   107         2.22      48.3 5.87e-200   103       112   
2 salt_g          3.36      0.29      11.6 7.20e- 28     2.79      3.93



t = estimate ÷ standard error — how many SEs from zero
p-value — if H₀ were true, the chance of a |t| this large or larger
95% CI = estimate ± ≈2 SE

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text: What a p-value looks like

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
section: What a p-value is — and is not
text:
What a p-value is — and is not



It is
the probability of data this extreme if β were truly 0 (and the model assumptions hold)



It is not

the probability that H₀ is true
the size or importance of the effect
a measure of whether the finding will replicate

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Confidence intervals say more

cbind(estimate = coef(m_adj), confint(m_adj))["salt_g", ] |> round(2)

estimate    2.5 %   97.5 % 
    1.80     1.21     2.39 



Adjusted salt effect: 1.8 mmHg per g/day (95% CI 1.2 to 2.4)
A CI shows size and precision; p only says whether 0 is excluded
CI excludes 0 ⇔ p < 0.05 (same information, richer format)

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Statistical vs clinical significance

# A tiny true effect: 0.5 mmHg per g/day, SD of salt = 2.3 g, residual SD = 15 mmHg
tibble(n = c(50, 200, 1000, 5000, 20000)) |>
  mutate(se = 15 / (2.3 * sqrt(n)), t = 0.5 / se, p = 2 * pt(-abs(t), n - 2)) |>
  mutate(across(c(se, t), ~ round(.x, 2)), p = signif(p, 2))

# A tibble: 5 × 4
      n    se     t        p
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>
1    50  0.92  0.54 5.9 e- 1
2   200  0.46  1.08 2.8 e- 1
3  1000  0.21  2.42 1.6 e- 2
4  5000  0.09  5.42 6.20e- 8
5 20000  0.05 10.8  2.6 e-27



With enough people, even an effect of 0.5 mmHg per g/day becomes “highly significant”. Ask two separate questions: Is it unlikely to be chance? (p) and Is it big enough to matter for patients or programmes? (effect size + CI).


Our adjusted effect is about 1.8 mmHg per g/day: a 5 g/day reduction in the community would shift mean SBP by about 9 mmHg — clinically large at population level. Judge size against what matters clinically, not against 0.05.

Crude vs adjusted β

m_crude <- lm(sbp ~ salt_g, data = cc)
m_adj   <- lm(sbp ~ salt_g + age + bmi + sex + residence + education +
                tobacco + alcohol + phys_act, data = cc)

c(crude = coef(m_crude)[["salt_g"]], adjusted = coef(m_adj)[["salt_g"]])

   crude adjusted 
3.357640 1.799679 

100 * (coef(m_crude)[["salt_g"]] - coef(m_adj)[["salt_g"]]) / coef(m_crude)[["salt_g"]]   # % change

[1] 46.40047




The salt β shrinks from 3.4 to 1.8 mmHg per g/day — 46% of the crude association was confounding. (Rule of thumb: ≥10% change ⇒ the variable matters as a confounder.)

text:
“Holding the others constant”

Adjusted β for salt = 1.8: compare two people of the same age, BMI, sex, residence, education, tobacco, alcohol and activity — the one who eats 1 g/day more has, on average, 1.8 mmHg higher SBP.

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Four ways to choose covariates








Strategy
Idea
Verdict




DAG / theory-driven
Choose covariates from causal knowledge before looking at p-values
⭐ Recommended


Purposeful selection
Screen, fit, drop, re-check change in β
Acceptable if confounding-focused


Forward / backward / stepwise (AIC)
Let an algorithm add and drop terms
⚠️ Exploration only


Univariable p < 0.2 screening
Keep what is “significant” alone
⚠️ Avoid (Session 6)

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Purposeful selection (Hosmer–Lemeshow)

Fit each variable alone; keep those clinically important or with a liberal p (≈ 0.20–0.25)
Fit the multivariable model with all of those
Remove variables that are non-significant and whose removal changes other β by < 10–20%
Add back any variable that changes the exposure β by ≥ 10–20% (confounder)
Check linearity and plausible interactions



It is driven by change in the exposure β, not only p-values — better than stepwise, but still data-driven.

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
DAG / theory-driven selection — recommended

This DAG is the team’s causal story, drawn before analysis. Orange = confounders to adjust for. Dashed = risk factors for the outcome only: adjusting for them improves precision but is not needed for confounding. DAGs are assumptions — state them, defend them, and show sensitivity to alternatives.

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
How theory chooses the model

Adjust for common causes of exposure and outcome (age, sex, residence, BMI-as-confounder, education)
Add outcome-only risk factors (tobacco, alcohol, activity) for precision
Do not adjust for mediators (on the path salt → … → SBP) or colliders
Pre-specify the model in your protocol; report it regardless of p-values



That is exactly the “adjusted” model we have been fitting — chosen from the diagram, not from the p-values.

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Automated selection: how step() works



Forward
start empty → add the term that lowers AIC most → stop when none helps



Backward
start full → drop the term whose removal lowers AIC most → stop when none helps



Both (stepwise)
at each step consider adding or dropping → stop when AIC cannot improve



AIC = fit penalised for number of parameters; lower is better. (Same data, same rows in every model!)

4 - residence  1     27.6       542    98723.4 2876.8

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Do they agree?

sel <- list(forward = fwd, backward = bwd, both = both, full = m_full)
map_dfr(sel, ~ {
  tl <- attr(terms(.x), "term.labels")
  tibble(n_terms = length(tl), AIC = round(AIC(.x), 1),
         salt_b = round(coef(.x)[["salt_g"]], 2),
         adiposity_kept = paste(intersect(c("bmi", "waist"), tl), collapse = " + "))
}, .id = "strategy")

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  strategy n_terms   AIC salt_b adiposity_kept
  <chr>      <int> <dbl>  <dbl> <chr>         
1 forward        7 4444.   1.83 waist         
2 backward       7 4442.   1.79 bmi           
3 both           7 4442.   1.79 bmi           
4 full          10 4451.   1.8  bmi + waist   



Forward kept waist; backward and both kept bmi — near-duplicates. Which “wins” is a coin flip, not science.

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Why automated selection is problematic



1. Biased β — selected variables look stronger than they are (winner’s curse)


2. Too-narrow CIs and p-values too small — they ignore that you searched



3. Unstable — a different sample selects different variables


4. Ignores confounding logic — can drop a confounder, keep a mediator, or pick waist over bmi by chance



Let us see 1–3 in our data.

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Demo 1: step() on pure noise

set.seed(1)
noise <- as_tibble(matrix(rnorm(nrow(cc) * 20), ncol = 20, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("z", 1:20))))
d_n   <- bind_cols(cc |> select(sbp, salt_g, age, bmi), noise)
kept  <- step(lm(sbp ~ ., data = d_n), trace = 0)

tidy(kept) |> filter(str_detect(term, "^z")) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  term  estimate std.error statistic p.value
  <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
1 z3      -0.926     0.588     -1.58   0.116
2 z4       0.986     0.54       1.82   0.069
3 z10     -0.9       0.63      -1.43   0.153
4 z17      1.27      0.62       2.05   0.041



Twenty random-number variables, nothing to find. step() kept 4 of them, one with p = 0.041. A thesis table built this way reports “significant” noise.

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
section: Demo 2: the selection changes with the sample
text:
Demo 2: the selection changes with the sample

set.seed(42)
vars <- c("salt_g", "age", "bmi", "waist", "sex", "residence", "education", "tobacco", "alcohol", "phys_act")
B <- 100
res <- map(seq_len(B), \(i) {
  bs <- cc[sample(nrow(cc), replace = TRUE), ]
  mm <- step(lm(reformulate(vars, "sbp"), bs), trace = 0)
  list(sel = vars %in% attr(terms(mm), "term.labels"),
       alc = if ("alcoholYes" %in% names(coef(mm))) coef(mm)[["alcoholYes"]] else 0)
})
freq <- tibble(variable = vars, selected = rowMeans(sapply(res, `[[`, "sel")))

ggplot(freq, aes(selected, reorder(variable, selected))) +
  geom_col(fill = col_blue) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(.5, 1), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "% of 100 bootstrap samples in which backward step() kept the variable", y = NULL)



Bootstrap = resample the same 550 people with replacement and rerun the whole procedure. Variables such as BMI, alcohol and education flip in and out; residence and waist are rarely selected. A “final model” from one run is one draw from this distribution.

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
section: Demo 2: the selection changes with the sample
text: Demo 2: the selection changes with the sample

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
section: Demo 3: the β after selection is distorted
text:
Demo 3: the β after selection is distorted

b_alc <- sapply(res, `[[`, "alc")
tibble(beta = b_alc) |>
  ggplot(aes(beta)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = col_blue, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = coef(m_full)[["alcoholYes"]], colour = col_red, linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "β for alcohol across 100 step() runs (0 = dropped)", y = "bootstrap samples")



Red line = full-model β (2.5). Alcohol survived in 64 of 100 runs; when kept, its average β was 3.7 — inflated; when dropped it is 0. One “final” model hides all of this, hence overly narrow CIs.

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
A defensible workflow

Think first — draw the DAG; list confounders; fix the model in the protocol
Fit crude and adjusted models; report both (tbl_merge)
Check assumptions (Session 4)
Sensitivity: alternative covariate sets (e.g., swap BMI ↔︎ waist)
Use step(), if at all, only to explore — and say so

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Self-check quiz (1/6)

The salt coefficient has p = 0.0003. Which statement is correct?

There is a 0.03% chance that the null hypothesis is true
Data this extreme would be rare if the true β were exactly 0
Salt explains 99.97% of the variation in systolic pressure
The effect of salt on blood pressure is clearly clinically important

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Self-check quiz (2/6)

The salt β falls from 3.4 (crude) to 1.8 after adjusting for age, BMI and others. What does this mainly suggest?

Salt has no effect on systolic pressure at all
Part of the crude association was due to confounding
The adjusted model contains too many variables
The crude model must have contained a calculation error

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Self-check quiz (3/6)

In the adjusted model with low activity as the reference, phys_acthigh = −5.0. What does this mean?

Each additional hour of weekly activity lowers a person’s SBP by 5.0 mmHg on average
High-activity adults average 5.0 mmHg less SBP than low-activity ones, others equal
Physical activity reduces systolic pressure by 5% in everyone who exercises more
High-activity adults are five times as common as low-activity adults in the sample

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Self-check quiz (4/6)

Which statement about stepwise (AIC) selection is TRUE?

It identifies the model with the most plausible causal structure in the data
The final p-values and CIs ignore the search, so they look too optimistic
It tends to pick the same variables in each resample of the dataset
It can never remove a variable that confounds the exposure-outcome link

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Self-check quiz (5/6)

An algorithm starts from an intercept-only model, adds the variable that most improves AIC at each step, and stops when none helps. What is this strategy called? (one word)

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Self-check quiz (6/6)

With low activity as reference, phys_actmoderate = −3.4 and phys_acthigh = −5.0. How many mmHg lower is mean SBP in the high group than in the moderate group, all else equal? (1 decimal)

title: Session 3 — Inference and Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Score and take-home
Your score: 

p answers “could this be chance?”; CI shows size and precision; ask “is it clinically meaningful?”
Confounding: compare crude vs adjusted β (≥10% change matters)
Dummy coding: k − 1 columns, each vs the reference — always name it
Choose covariates from theory (DAG), not from p-values; step() is exploration only

Next: Session 4 — are the model’s assumptions believable?

title: Session 1 — Foundations
text:
Our running example

“Does eating more salt raise blood pressure in our community — and by how much?”


A simulated NCD survey: 600 adults aged 30–69 across 20 villages in an Indian community setting
Outcomes: systolic BP (continuous) and hypertension (yes/no)
Exposure of interest: daily salt intake (g/day)
Other variables: age, sex, residence, education, BMI, waist, tobacco, alcohol, physical activity
All six sessions and labs use the same dataset


The data are simulated so that every teaching point (confounding, collinearity, non-constant variance, clustering, common outcome, missing values) shows up on cue. Do not mention individual features yet — we will discover them.

title: Session 1 — Foundations
text:
What is regression?

Regression describes how the average value of an outcome changes with one or more predictors.




“Among adults who eat 8 g of salt a day, the average SBP is …”
“For each extra 1 g/day of salt, average SBP is … mmHg higher”
One equation gives description, comparison and prediction

title: Session 1 — Foundations
text:
Why do we use regression?



Describe an association with a number in real units
Adjust for other factors (age, BMI …) — the key idea in observational public health research
Predict an outcome for a new person or community
Test a hypothesis with a confidence interval



Why not just a t-test or chi-square?

They compare groups, one variable at a time
Regression handles continuous exposures, many variables at once, and gives an effect size (not only a p-value)

title: Session 1 — Foundations
text:
Regression in community medicine








Public health question
Outcome
Typical model




Is household wealth associated with child haemoglobin (NFHS)?
Hb (g/dL) – continuous
Linear


Which factors predict hypertension in a screening camp?
Hypertension – binary
Logistic


Rainfall and monthly dengue cases per ward
Count
Poisson / neg. binomial


Stage of diabetic retinopathy and duration of diabetes
Ordered categories
Ordinal logistic


Time to treatment failure in DOTS patients
Time-to-event
Cox


Blood pressure of patients repeated across visits in one PHC
Repeated measures
Mixed model / GEE




Ask the audience for their own thesis topics and place each on this table. The right-most column is the thread of the whole day.

Correlation vs regression: the differences

cor(ncd$sbp, ncd$salt_g, use = "complete.obs")        # symmetric, unit-free

[1] 0.4489003

coef(lm(sbp ~ salt_g, data = ncd))["salt_g"]           # directional, in mmHg per g

  salt_g 
3.389337 

coef(lm(salt_g ~ sbp, data = ncd))["sbp"]              # swap the roles -> a different slope

       sbp 
0.05945456 






Correlation (r)
Regression (β)




Roles of X and Y
Symmetric
Outcome and predictor


Units
None (−1 to +1)
Outcome units per predictor unit


Adjust for other variables
No
Yes


Predict new values
No
Yes

title: Session 1 — Foundations
text:
Dependent vs independent variables








Role
Also called
In our survey




Dependent variable
outcome, response, Y
SBP, hypertension


Independent variable
predictor, exposure, X, covariate
salt intake, age, BMI …


Confounder
adjustment variable
age, BMI (related to salt and SBP)





“Dependent” is a modelling role, not a statement of causation. The same variable can be an outcome in one analysis and a predictor in another (BMI!).

title: Session 1 — Foundations
section: Type of outcome decides the model
text:
Type of outcome decides the model


Continuous

SBP (mmHg), BMI, Hb
Summarised by mean ± SD
→ linear regression


Categorical

Binary: hypertension yes/no
Nominal: facility chosen (PHC / CHC / private)
Ordinal: BP stage 1 / 2 / 3
Plus counts and time-to-event




The first question in any regression analysis is not “which software?” but “what type of outcome do I have?”

title: Quarto — Publication
text:
Journal-Quality Documents
A well-structured YAML for a manuscript-style document:
---
title: "Effect of Clean Fuel Intervention on Blood Pressure: A Community Trial"
author:
  - name: "Dr. Mukul Maheshwari"
    affiliation: "Department of Community Medicine"
    email: "author@institution.ac.in"
  - name: "Dr. Rudresh Negi"
    affiliation: "Department of Community Medicine"
date: today
abstract: |
  **Background:** Indoor air pollution remains a major public health concern...
  **Methods:** A cluster-randomised trial was conducted...
  **Results:** ...
  **Conclusion:** ...
keywords: [indoor air pollution, blood pressure, community trial, R]
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
    number-sections: true
    theme: flatly
  pdf:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true
    cite-method: biblatex
    pdf-engine: xelatex
    mainfont: "Times New Roman"
    fontsize: 12pt
    geometry: "margin=2.5cm"
bibliography: references.bib
csl: vancouver.csl          # citation style (download from Zotero CSL repo)
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
---

Callouts draw attention to key information without disrupting text flow.

title: Quarto — Publication
text:
Multi-File Quarto Projects

Books
A Quarto book renders multiple .qmd files into a single structured document (HTML, PDF, or ePub).
my-book/
├── _quarto.yml
├── index.qmd        (preface / front matter)
├── 01-intro.qmd
├── 02-methods.qmd
├── 03-results.qmd
├── 04-discussion.qmd
└── references.qmd
_quarto.yml for a book:
project:
  type: book

book:
  title: "Community Trial Methods in R"
  author: "Dr. Mukul Maheshwari"
  date: today
  chapters:
    - index.qmd
    - 01-intro.qmd
    - 02-methods.qmd
    - 03-results.qmd
    - 04-discussion.qmd
    - references.qmd

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
  pdf:
    documentclass: scrbook


Websites
For a multi-page website (like this workshop), see the project’s _quarto.yml for a working example of navbar configuration, profiles, and output directories.

title: Quarto — Publication
text:
GitHub + Quarto Publishing Workflow

Option A — Push rendered HTML to GitHub Pages

Render your project locally: quarto render
Output goes to docs/ (set output-dir: docs in _quarto.yml)
Commit and push the docs/ folder to GitHub
In your repository: Settings → Pages → Source → Branch: main, Folder: /docs

# Full publish cycle
quarto render
git add docs/
git commit -m "Rebuild site"
git push


Option B — GitHub Actions (automated rebuild)
Create .github/workflows/publish.yml:
name: Publish Quarto Site

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies@v2
        with:
          packages: |
            any::quarto
            any::tidyverse
            any::ggstatsplot
            any::gtsummary

      - uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2

      - name: Render and publish
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2
        with:
          target: gh-pages
With this workflow, every push to main automatically rebuilds and deploys the site.


Option C — Quarto Pub (zero configuration)
quarto publish quarto-pub
Creates a free public site at username.quarto.pub/project-name. Suitable for sharing documents without managing a GitHub repository.

title: Quarto — Publication
text:
Embedding Shiny in Quarto
For lightweight interactivity within a static Quarto document.

Using shinylive (no server required)
shinylive compiles Shiny to WebAssembly — no Shiny server needed.
---
title: "Interactive Report"
format: html
filters:
  - shinylive
---
```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
library(shiny)
library(ggplot2)

ui <- fluidPage(
  sliderInput("bins", "Bins:", 5, 50, 20),
  plotOutput("hist")
)

server <- function(input, output) {
  output$hist <- renderPlot({
```

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
ggwithinstats() — Repeated Measures
Use this when the same participants are measured more than once (paired/within-subjects design) — for example, pre-post measurements.

library(ggstatsplot)
library(tidyr)

# Reshape from wide to long for within-subjects comparison
overall_long <- overall_up |>
  select(member_id, sbp_0m, sbp_3m) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(sbp_0m, sbp_3m),
    names_to  = "timepoint",
    values_to = "sbp"
  ) |>
  mutate(timepoint = factor(timepoint,
                            levels = c("sbp_0m", "sbp_3m"),
                            labels = c("Baseline", "3 Months")))

ggwithinstats(
  data    = overall_long,
  x       = timepoint,
  y       = sbp,
  subject.id = member_id,       # links pairs across timepoints
  title   = "Systolic BP: Baseline vs 3 Months"
)

Key differences from ggbetweenstats():

subject.id is required — it tells the function which rows are paired
Uses a paired t-test (parametric) or Wilcoxon signed-rank (non-parametric)
Lines connect paired observations in the plot

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
ggbarstats() — Proportions
Use this when you want to compare proportions of a categorical outcome across groups. The output includes a χ² or Fisher’s exact test.

ggbarstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = fuel_type,           # grouping variable (x-axis)
  y     = tobacco_type,        # outcome category (fill)
  title = "Tobacco Type by Fuel Type"
)

What the output shows:

Stacked bar chart with proportion labels
χ² test statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and Cramér’s V effect size
Pairwise comparisons between bars (if > 2 groups)

Swap axes to change orientation:

# Make tobacco_type the grouping variable
ggbarstats(data = overall_up, x = tobacco_type, y = fuel_type)

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
ggpiestats() — Pie / Donut Charts
Use this for a single categorical variable, or two categorical variables where a pie chart is appropriate for the audience.

# Single variable — proportions of intervention types
ggpiestats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = intervention,
  title = "Distribution of Intervention Groups"
)


# Two variables — tobacco type by intervention
ggpiestats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = tobacco_type,
  y     = intervention,       # creates faceted pies
  title = "Tobacco Type by Intervention"
)







WarningWhen to use pie charts



Pie charts are appropriate when there are ≤ 5 categories and the audience is non-technical. For more categories or detailed comparisons, prefer ggbarstats().

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
Customising appearance
All ggstatsplot functions return a ggplot2 object, so you can extend them normally.

library(ggplot2)

ggbetweenstats(
  data        = overall_up,
  x           = fuel_type,
  y           = sbp_0m,
  # Colours for each group
  palette     = "Set2",
  package     = "RColorBrewer",
  # Remove the subtitle (statistical results) if preferred
  results.subtitle = TRUE,
  # Change point size and transparency
  point.args  = list(size = 2, alpha = 0.4),
  title       = "Systolic BP by Fuel Type"
) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  labs(caption = "Source: NCTOH Study Dataset")

Common customisation parameters:



Parameter
What it controls




palette + package
Colour palette for groups


results.subtitle
Show/hide statistical annotation


point.args
Size, alpha, shape of data points


centrality.plotting
Show/hide mean/median marker


xlab / ylab
Axis labels

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
Introduction to Bayes Factors
When you set type = "bayes", ggstatsplot reports a Bayes Factor (BF₁₀) instead of a p-value.

ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = fuel_type,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  type  = "bayes",
  title = "Systolic BP by Fuel Type (Bayesian)"
)

Interpreting BF₁₀:



BF₁₀
Interpretation




> 100
Extreme evidence for H₁


30–100
Very strong evidence for H₁


10–30
Strong evidence for H₁


3–10
Moderate evidence for H₁


1–3
Anecdotal evidence for H₁


~1
No evidence either way


1/3–1
Anecdotal evidence for H₀


< 1/10
Strong–extreme evidence for H₀




BF₁₀ > 3: reasonably confident that H₁ (an effect exists) is supported
BF₁₀ < 1/3: reasonably confident that H₀ (no effect) is supported
Values between 1/3 and 3 are inconclusive







Note



Bayesian inference and deeper interpretation of Bayes factors is covered in ggstatsplot — Advanced.

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
Bayesian Reporting Workflow
The Bayesian approach in ggstatsplot uses the BayesFactor package internally. The goal is to quantify how much evidence exists for or against an effect, rather than simply crossing a significance threshold.

Setting priors

library(ggstatsplot)

# Default Cauchy prior (r = 0.707) — appropriate for most comparisons
ggbetweenstats(
  data         = overall_up,
  x            = intervention,
  y            = sbp_0m,
  type         = "bayes",
  bf.prior     = 0.707,        # scale of Cauchy prior on effect size
  title        = "SBP by Intervention (Bayesian, default prior)"
)

# Narrow prior — use if you expect a small effect
ggbetweenstats(
  data         = overall_up,
  x            = intervention,
  y            = sbp_0m,
  type         = "bayes",
  bf.prior     = 0.5,
  title        = "SBP by Intervention (narrow prior)"
)



Reporting Bayes factors in text
When BF₁₀ = 18.4:

“A Bayesian independent-samples t-test revealed moderate-to-strong evidence for a difference in baseline SBP between intervention groups, BF₁₀ = 18.4, δ = 0.41, 95% credible interval [0.18, 0.65].”

When BF₁₀ = 0.21:

“A Bayesian independent-samples t-test provided moderate evidence in favour of the null hypothesis (no difference in SBP), BF₁₀ = 0.21.”







TipKey distinction: BF₁₀ vs BF₀₁




BF₁₀: evidence for H₁ over H₀ (use when testing for an effect)
BF₀₁ = 1/BF₁₀: evidence for H₀ over H₁ (use when supporting the null)

ggstatsplot reports BF₁₀ by default. To interpret support for H₀, invert it.

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
grouped_* Functions — Faceted Comparisons
The grouped_* variants run the same comparison separately within each level of a grouping variable and combine the results into a faceted plot.

# Compare SBP across tobacco types, separately by sex
grouped_ggbetweenstats(
  data             = overall_up,
  x                = tobacco_type,
  y                = sbp_0m,
  grouping.var     = sex,           # one panel per sex
  title            = "SBP by Tobacco Type, stratified by Sex",
  plotgrid.args    = list(ncol = 2)
)


# Correlation stratified by intervention group
grouped_ggscatterstats(
  data         = overall_up,
  x            = current_age,
  y            = sbp_0m,
  grouping.var = intervention,
  title        = "Age vs SBP by Intervention Group"
)

Available grouped functions:

grouped_ggbetweenstats()
grouped_ggwithinstats()
grouped_ggscatterstats()
grouped_gghistostats()
grouped_ggbarstats()
grouped_ggpiestats()
grouped_ggcorrmat()
grouped_ggdotplotstats()

ggcorrmat() — Correlation Matrix
Visualises pairwise correlations across multiple continuous variables with significance annotations.

ggcorrmat(
  data   = overall_up |> select(current_age, sbp_0m, sbp_3m, sbp_6m,
                                 consumption_per_day_0m),
  title  = "Correlation Matrix — Baseline Variables",
  type   = "parametric"     # "parametric", "nonparametric", "robust", "bayes"
)

Choosing the correlation type:



type
Method
When to use




"parametric"
Pearson’s r
Continuous, approximately normal


"nonparametric"
Spearman’s ρ
Ordinal or skewed distributions


"robust"
Percentage bend r
Presence of outliers


"bayes"

Quantify evidence, not just significance

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced

Combining with patchwork
All ggstatsplot outputs are ggplot2 objects and compose naturally with patchwork.

library(patchwork)

p1 <- ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = intervention,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  title = "Baseline SBP"
)

p2 <- ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = intervention,
  y     = sbp_3m,
  title = "3-Month SBP"
)

p3 <- ggscatterstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = sbp_0m,
  y     = sbp_3m,
  title = "Baseline vs 3-Month SBP"
)

# Compose: two plots on top, one full-width below
(p1 | p2) / p3 +
  plot_annotation(
    title   = "Blood Pressure Outcomes by Intervention",
    caption = "Source: NCTOH Study Dataset"
  )

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
Publication-ready output

library(ggplot2)

pub_plot <- ggbetweenstats(
  data             = overall_up,
  x                = intervention,
  y                = sbp_0m,
  type             = "parametric",
  pairwise.display = "significant",    # show only significant comparisons
  p.adjust.method  = "bonferroni",
  title            = "Baseline Systolic Blood Pressure by Intervention Group",
  xlab             = "Intervention Group",
  ylab             = "Systolic BP (mmHg)",
  package          = "RColorBrewer",
  palette          = "Set1"
) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.line        = element_line(linewidth = 0.5),
    plot.caption     = element_text(hjust = 0, colour = "grey50")
  ) +
  labs(caption = "Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons shown for p < 0.05")

# Save at print quality
ggsave("figures/sbp_by_intervention.png",
       pub_plot, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300)

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
Case Study: Healthcare Data
A complete example using the NCTOH study dataset — comparing the change in SBP across intervention groups, accounting for tobacco type.

library(ggstatsplot)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)

# Derive SBP change variable
study_data <- overall_up |>
  mutate(sbp_change = sbp_3m - sbp_0m)

# 1. Overall change by intervention
p_overall <- ggbetweenstats(
  data  = study_data,
  x     = intervention,
  y     = sbp_change,
  type  = "parametric",
  title = "Change in SBP at 3 Months"
)

# 2. Stratified by tobacco type
p_strat <- grouped_ggbetweenstats(
  data         = study_data,
  x            = intervention,
  y            = sbp_change,
  grouping.var = tobacco_type,
  title        = "SBP Change Stratified by Tobacco Type",
  plotgrid.args = list(ncol = 3)
)

# View each
p_overall
p_strat

title: Exporting plots
text: Exporting plots from R can be done in several ways, depending on the desired output format and quality. Here are some common methods to export plots:

title: Exporting plots
text:
Using R’s Built-in Functions
R provides several built-in functions for exporting plots to different formats:

Raster Formats

png(), jpeg(), tiff(), bmp(): These functions save plots in raster formats. You can specify filename, dimensions, and resolution.

# PNG format (good for web)
png("plot.png", width = 800, height = 600, res = 100)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

# High-resolution TIFF for publications
tiff("plot.tiff", width = 8, height = 6, units = "in", res = 300)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()


Vector Formats

pdf(): Saves plots in PDF format, vector-based and scalable.
svg(): Saves plots in SVG format, ideal for web and scalable graphics.

# PDF for high-quality prints
pdf("plot.pdf", width = 8, height = 6)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

# SVG for web use
svg("plot.svg", width = 8, height = 6)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

title: Exporting plots
text:
Exporting ggplot2 Plots
For ggplot2 plots, the ggsave() function is the most convenient way to export:
library(ggplot2)

# Create a plot
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point()

# Save in different formats
ggsave("plot.png", p, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 150)
ggsave("plot.pdf", p, width = 8, height = 6)
ggsave("plot.svg", p, width = 8, height = 6)

Controlling Output Quality

Resolution (DPI): Higher DPI for print quality (300+), lower for web (72-150)
Dimensions: Specify in inches or pixels
Aspect Ratio: Maintain proportions for consistency

# High-resolution for publications
ggsave("publication_plot.tiff", p, 
       width = 6, height = 4, 
       dpi = 300, 
       device = "tiff")

# Web-optimized PNG
ggsave("web_plot.png", p, 
       width = 800, height = 600, 
       dpi = 100, 
       units = "px")

title: Exporting plots
text:
Advanced Exporting Techniques

Exporting Multiple Plots
# Save multiple plots to PDF
pdf("multiple_plots.pdf")
plot1 <- ggplot(data1, aes(x, y)) + geom_point()
print(plot1)
plot2 <- ggplot(data2, aes(x, y)) + geom_line()
print(plot2)
dev.off()


Using Cairo for Better Quality
The Cairo graphics library can provide better quality for some formats:
install.packages("Cairo")
library(Cairo)

CairoPNG("high_quality.png", width = 800, height = 600)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()


Exporting to Clipboard
For quick sharing:
# Windows
savePlot("clipboard", type = "wmf")

# Or for ggplot2
ggsave("clipboard", p, device = "png")

title: Exporting plots
text:
Best Practices

Choose the right format: PDF/SVG for vector graphics, PNG/TIFF for raster
Set appropriate resolution: 300 DPI for print, 72-150 for screen
Consider file size: Vector formats scale better but may be larger
Test outputs: Always check exported files in target applications
Use consistent dimensions: Maintain aspect ratios across exports

title: Exporting plots
text:
Common Issues and Solutions

Plot not saving: Ensure dev.off() is called after plotting
Low quality: Increase DPI or use vector formats
Wrong dimensions: Specify units explicitly (inches, cm, pixels)
Colors not matching: Check color profiles and device settings

title: Advanced Exporting Techniques
text:
This chapter covers advanced techniques for exporting plots, including programmatic generation, batch processing, custom devices, and integration with other tools.




library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)

# Create plots for each cylinder group
plots <- mtcars %>%
  split(.$cyl) %>%
  map(~ ggplot(.x, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + 
        geom_point() + 
        ggtitle(paste("Cylinders:", .x$cyl[1])))

# Save each plot
walk2(plots, names(plots), 
      ~ ggsave(filename = paste0("plot_cyl_", .x, ".png"), 
               plot = .y, 
               width = 6, height = 4))



# Generate timestamped filenames
timestamp <- format(Sys.time(), "%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")

ggsave(paste0("analysis_plot_", timestamp, ".pdf"), 
       plot = p, 
       width = 8, height = 6)






save_plot_multiple_formats <- function(plot, filename_base, 
                                     formats = c("png", "pdf", "svg")) {
  for (fmt in formats) {
    filename <- paste0(filename_base, ".", fmt)
    ggsave(filename, plot, width = 8, height = 6)
  }
}

# Usage
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
save_plot_multiple_formats(p, "mtcars_scatter")



datasets <- list(
  mtcars = mtcars,
  iris = iris,
  airquality = airquality
)

for (name in names(datasets)) {
  data <- datasets[[name]]
  # Create appropriate plot based on data
  if (name == "mtcars") {
    p <- ggplot(data, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
  } else if (name == "iris") {
    p <- ggplot(data, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width, color = Species)) + 
      geom_point()
  }
  
  ggsave(paste0(name, "_plot.png"), p, width = 6, height = 4)
}






library(Cairo)

# High-quality PNG
CairoPNG("high_quality.png", width = 800, height = 600, 
         bg = "white", pointsize = 12)
plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
dev.off()

# PDF with embedded fonts
CairoPDF("embedded_fonts.pdf", width = 8, height = 6, 
         family = "Arial")
plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
dev.off()



# Create a custom device wrapper
save_high_res <- function(filename, plot_func, ...) {
  png(filename, width = 1200, height = 800, res = 150, ...)
  plot_func()
  dev.off()
}

# Usage
my_plot <- function() {
  plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg, 
       xlab = "Weight", ylab = "MPG",
       main = "High Resolution Plot")
}

save_high_res("high_res_plot.png", my_plot)






library(tikzDevice)

# Export as TikZ for LaTeX
tikz("plot.tex", width = 4, height = 3)
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
dev.off()



# Export as HTML with plotly
library(plotly)
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(ggplotly(p), "interactive_plot.html")






# Create publication-ready theme
publication_theme <- theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 12, family = "Times"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point() +
  publication_theme +
  labs(title = "Publication Quality Plot")

ggsave("publication_plot.pdf", p, 
       width = 6, height = 4, 
       device = cairo_pdf)



library(cowplot)

# Create individual plots
p1 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
p2 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)) + geom_boxplot()
p3 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = hp)) + geom_histogram()

# Combine into single figure
combined <- plot_grid(p1, p2, p3, 
                      labels = c("A", "B", "C"),
                      ncol = 2)

# Save combined figure
ggsave("combined_figure.pdf", combined, 
       width = 10, height = 8)






# For large datasets, use sampling or aggregation
large_data <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100000), y = rnorm(100000))

# Option 1: Sample data
sample_data <- large_data[sample(nrow(large_data), 10000), ]
ggplot(sample_data, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.1)
ggsave("sampled_plot.png")

# Option 2: Use density plots
ggplot(large_data, aes(x = x, y = y)) + 
  geom_density2d() +
  geom_point(data = sample_data, alpha = 0.1)
ggsave("density_plot.png")



# Clear graphics devices
graphics.off()

# Force garbage collection
gc()

# Monitor memory usage
library(pryr)
mem_used()






check_plot_quality <- function(filename) {
  # Check file exists
  if (!file.exists(filename)) {
    stop("File was not created")
  }
  
  # Check file size (basic quality indicator)
  size <- file.info(filename)$size
  if (size < 1000) {
    warning("File seems too small, may indicate error")
  }
  
  # For images, could check dimensions
  if (grepl("\\.png$", filename)) {
    img <- png::readPNG(filename)
    message("Image dimensions: ", dim(img)[1], "x", dim(img)[2])
  }
}

# Usage
ggsave("test_plot.png", ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point())
check_plot_quality("test_plot.png")





Automate repetitive tasks: Use functions and loops for batch processing
Standardize formats: Establish consistent dimensions and resolutions
Quality control: Implement checks for successful exports
Performance awareness: Optimize for large datasets
Version control: Track plot versions with timestamps or git
Documentation: Comment code for reproducible exports
Cross-platform compatibility: Test exports on target systems

title: Regression Analysis
text:
Regression Diagnostics
A fitted model is only trustworthy once its assumptions have been checked.

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model)









# Residuals vs fitted, and a normal Q-Q check
qqnorm(residuals(model))
qqline(residuals(model), col = "red")








Watch for: non-random patterns in residuals-vs-fitted (non-linearity), points far off the Q-Q line (non-normal residuals), and high-leverage points in the residuals-vs-leverage panel.
