title: Data Analysis
text:
Why Check Normality?
Many parametric tests (t-test, ANOVA, Pearson’s r) assume normally distributed data.
Failing to check normality can lead to:

Invalid p-values
Wrong test selection
Misleading conclusions

Two approaches: Visual methods + Statistical tests

title: Data Analysis
text:
Visual Methods — Histogram

hist(
  p$age_of_participants,
  main  = "Histogram with Density Line",
  xlab  = "Age",
  ylab  = "Density",
  col   = "grey",
  border = "black",
  freq  = FALSE
)
lines(density(p$age_of_participants), col = "red", lwd = 2)


A roughly bell-shaped curve suggests normality. Skewed or multimodal histograms indicate non-normality.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Visual Methods — QQ Plot

qqnorm(p$sbp_in_mm_hg, main = "Q-Q Plot: SBP")
qqline(p$sbp_in_mm_hg, col = "red")


Points should follow the red diagonal line closely if the data are normally distributed. Deviations at the tails indicate non-normality.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Statistical Tests — Shapiro-Wilk
Best for small samples (n ≤ 50). Randomly sample if n > 50.

p1 <- p[sample(nrow(p), 50), ]
s_test <- shapiro.test(p1$age_of_participants)
s_test


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  p1$age_of_participants
W = 0.95544, p-value = 0.05732



Interpretation: p > 0.05 → data does not significantly deviate from normality (cannot reject H₀ of normality).

title: Data Analysis
text:
Statistical Tests — Kolmogorov-Smirnov
Suitable for larger samples. Compares distribution to a theoretical normal.

ks_test <- ks.test(p$sbp_in_mm_hg, "pnorm",
                   mean = mean(p$sbp_in_mm_hg),
                   sd   = sd(p$sbp_in_mm_hg))
ks_test


    Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  p$sbp_in_mm_hg
D = 0.052082, p-value = 0.06522
alternative hypothesis: two-sided



Note: Use options(scipen = 999) to display p-values in decimal format instead of scientific notation.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Statistical Tests — Anderson-Darling
More sensitive to tails than KS test. Requires nortest package.

ad_test <- ad.test(p$height)
ad_test


    Anderson-Darling normality test

data:  p$height
A = 0.27928, p-value = 0.6458





Test
Best Use
Package




Shapiro-Wilk
n ≤ 50
base R


Kolmogorov-Smirnov
n > 50, continuous
base R


Anderson-Darling
Sensitive to tail deviations
nortest

title: Data Analysis
text:
Decision Framework — Categorical






Note


Flowchart placeholder
Insert here: Categorical variable test selection flowchart — branching from number of groups (1, 2, >2) and paired vs unpaired, leading to: Chi-square goodness of fit → Chi-square test of independence / Fisher’s exact → McNemar / Exact McNemar → Chi-square m×n / Monte Carlo.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit — 1 Group
Tests whether the observed distribution matches an expected distribution.

observed <- table(p$ever_screened_for_bp)
total    <- sum(observed)
expected <- c(1/2, 1/2) * total

chisq_test <- chisq.test(x = observed, p = expected / sum(expected))
chisq_test


    Chi-squared test for given probabilities

data:  observed
X-squared = 80.23, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16



Assumption: Expected frequency ≥ 5 in each cell.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Chi-Square Test — 2 Binary Groups (Expected ≥ 5)
Tests association between two categorical variables using a contingency table.

table_gender_dm <- table(p$sex_of_participants, p$past_history_of_diabetes)
table_gender_dm

        
          no yes
  female 332  17
  male   265  17

chisq_m5 <- chisq.test(table_gender_dm, correct = FALSE)
chisq_m5


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  table_gender_dm
X-squared = 0.40978, df = 1, p-value = 0.5221

# Check expected frequencies
chisq_m5$expected

        
               no      yes
  female 330.1949 18.80507
  male   266.8051 15.19493



Use correct = FALSE to apply the standard Pearson Chi-square (no Yates correction).

title: Data Analysis
text:
Chi-Square — Yates Continuity Correction
Yates correction subtracts 0.5 from the absolute difference between observed and expected frequency before squaring.

# With Yates correction (correct = TRUE is default for 2x2 tables)
chisq.test(table_gender_dm, correct = TRUE)


    Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction

data:  table_gender_dm
X-squared = 0.2142, df = 1, p-value = 0.6435



Apply when sample sizes are small or expected frequencies approach 5.

title: Data Analysis
text:
When Expected Frequency < 5
Two options: Monte Carlo simulation or Fisher’s Exact Test.

table_htn_dm <- table(p$ever_screened_for_bp, p$past_history_of_diabetes)

# Monte Carlo simulation (B = number of replicates, min p = 1/(B+1))
chisq_mc <- chisq.test(table_htn_dm, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 2000)
chisq_mc


    Pearson's Chi-squared test with simulated p-value (based on 2000
    replicates)

data:  table_htn_dm
X-squared = 11.381, df = NA, p-value = 0.001499

# Fisher's Exact Test
fisher_test <- fisher.test(table_htn_dm)
fisher_test


    Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data

data:  table_htn_dm
p-value = 0.0002606
alternative hypothesis: true odds ratio is not equal to 1
95 percent confidence interval:
  2.032418 70.633884
sample estimates:
odds ratio 
  8.105124

title: Data Analysis
text:
Chi-Square — m × n Contingency Table
Use when both variables have more than two categories.

table_mar_wealth <- table(
  p$marital_status_of_participants,
  p$wealth_index_of_participants
)
table_mar_wealth

                       
                        middle poorer poorest richer richest
  currently married         82     68      17    119     115
  formerly/ever married     31     16      13     22      14
  never married             34     22       4     36      38

chisq_mn <- chisq.test(table_mar_wealth)
chisq_mn


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  table_mar_wealth
X-squared = 26.65, df = 8, p-value = 0.0008122

# Monte Carlo if expected frequencies < 5
chisq_mn_mc <- chisq.test(table_mar_wealth, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 2000)
chisq_mn_mc


    Pearson's Chi-squared test with simulated p-value (based on 2000
    replicates)

data:  table_mar_wealth
X-squared = 26.65, df = NA, p-value = 0.001999

title: Data Analysis
text:
McNemar Test — Paired Binary Responses
Use when the same participants are measured twice on a binary outcome (e.g., before and after treatment).

table_bfr_aftr <- table(p$pain_foot_bfr, p$pain_foot_aftr)
table_bfr_aftr

     
       No Yes
  No  176 159
  Yes 150 146

mcnemar_test <- mcnemar.test(table_bfr_aftr)
mcnemar_test


    McNemar's Chi-squared test with continuity correction

data:  table_bfr_aftr
McNemar's chi-squared = 0.20712, df = 1, p-value = 0.649



Assumption: Discordant cells (b + c) should be ≥ 25. If < 25, use exact McNemar.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Exact McNemar Test

exact_mcnemar <- exact2x2::mcnemar.exact(table_bfr_aftr)
exact_mcnemar


    Exact McNemar test (with central confidence intervals)

data:  table_bfr_aftr
b = 159, c = 150, p-value = 0.6491
alternative hypothesis: true odds ratio is not equal to 1
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.8426767 1.3339030
sample estimates:
odds ratio 
      1.06 





Situation
Test




Paired binary, discordant ≥ 25
McNemar


Paired binary, discordant < 5
Exact McNemar (exact2x2)

title: Data Analysis
text:
Decision Framework — Continuous






Note


Flowchart placeholder
Insert here: Continuous variable test selection flowchart — branching from number of groups (1, 2, >2), then normality (normal vs non-normal), then paired vs unpaired, leading to: Z-test / One-sample t → Independent t / Paired t / Mann-Whitney U / Wilcoxon Matched Pairs → One-way ANOVA / Repeated Measures ANOVA / Kruskal-Wallis / Friedman.

title: Data Analysis
text:
One Group — Z Test
Use when population SD is known and n > 30.

pr  <- p |> filter(wealth_index_of_participants == "richer")
mu  <- mean(p$age_of_participants)
sigma <- sd(p$age_of_participants)

s_mean <- mean(pr$age_of_participants)
n      <- length(pr$age_of_participants)
z      <- (s_mean - mu) / (sigma / sqrt(n))

p_two_tailed     <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z)))
p_one_tailed_gt  <- 1 - pnorm(z)
p_one_tailed_lt  <- pnorm(z)

cat("Z =", round(z, 3),
    "\nTwo-tailed p =", round(p_two_tailed, 4),
    "\nOne-tailed (greater) p =", round(p_one_tailed_gt, 4))

Z = -0.879 
Two-tailed p = 0.3794 
One-tailed (greater) p = 0.8103

title: Data Analysis
text:
One Group — One-Sample t Test
Use when population SD is unknown or n < 30.

pp <- p |> filter(wealth_index_of_participants == "poorest")

t_test <- t.test(pp$age_of_participants, mu = mu)
t_test


    One Sample t-test

data:  pp$age_of_participants
t = 1.5716, df = 33, p-value = 0.1256
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 43.84786
95 percent confidence interval:
 42.28702 56.00709
sample estimates:
mean of x 
 49.14706 





Test
Population SD
n




One-sample Z
Known
> 30


One-sample t
Unknown
Any; especially < 30

title: Data Analysis
text:
Two Groups — Testing Equal Variance
Before an independent t-test, verify the equal variance assumption.

# Levene's test (robust to non-normality)
car::leveneTest(weight ~ sex_of_participants, data = p)

Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median)
       Df F value Pr(>F)
group   1  0.0453 0.8316
      629               

# Bartlett's test (assumes normality)
bartlett.test(weight ~ sex_of_participants, data = p)


    Bartlett test of homogeneity of variances

data:  weight by sex_of_participants
Bartlett's K-squared = 0.21685, df = 1, p-value = 0.6415



Interpretation: p < 0.05 → variances are NOT equal → use var.equal = FALSE in t.test.

title: Data Analysis
section: Two Groups — Independent t Test (Unpaired, Normal)
text:
Two Groups — Independent t Test (Unpaired, Normal)

ind_t_test <- t.test(weight ~ sex_of_participants,
                     var.equal = TRUE,
                     data = p)
ind_t_test


    Two Sample t-test

data:  weight by sex_of_participants
t = 0.61333, df = 629, p-value = 0.5399
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group female and group male is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -1.662463  3.172588
sample estimates:
mean in group female   mean in group male 
            70.04272             69.28766 








Note


Flowchart placeholder
Insert here: Equal variance flowchart — Levene/Bartlett test → p < 0.05 (unequal variances, Welch t-test) vs p ≥ 0.05 (equal variances, standard independent t-test).

title: Data Analysis
text:
Two Groups — Paired t Test (Normal)
Use when the same participants are measured at two time points.

paired_t_test <- t.test(p$fbs_presentation, p$fbs_6_months, paired = TRUE)
paired_t_test


    Paired t-test

data:  p$fbs_presentation and p$fbs_6_months
t = 26.186, df = 630, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 14.06450 16.34501
sample estimates:
mean difference 
       15.20475 



Assumption: Differences between paired observations must be normally distributed.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Two Groups — Mann-Whitney U (Non-Normal, Unpaired)
Non-parametric alternative to the independent t-test. Based on ranks, not raw values.

mann_whit <- wilcox.test(sbp_presentation ~ sex_of_participants,
                         data = p,
                         correct = FALSE)
mann_whit


    Wilcoxon rank sum test

data:  sbp_presentation by sex_of_participants
W = 51423, p-value = 0.3308
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0



Use correct = TRUE (continuity correction) when: sample size < 100, or data is ordinal/discrete.

title: Data Analysis
section: Two Groups — Wilcoxon Matched Pairs (Non-Normal, Paired)
text:
Two Groups — Wilcoxon Matched Pairs (Non-Normal, Paired)
Non-parametric alternative to the paired t-test.

wilcox_paired <- wilcox.test(p$sbp_presentation, p$sbp_6_months, paired = TRUE)
wilcox_paired


    Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction

title: Data Analysis
text:
Repeated Measures ANOVA (Normal, Paired)
Use when the same participants are measured at three or more time points.

p_long_n <- p |>
  select(s_no, fbs_presentation, fbs_3_months, fbs_6_months) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(fbs_presentation, fbs_3_months, fbs_6_months),
    names_to = "time",
    values_to = "value"
  )

res_aov <- anova_test(data = p_long_n, dv = value, wid = s_no, within = time)
get_anova_table(res_aov)

ANOVA Table (type III tests)

  Effect DFn  DFd       F         p p<.05   ges
1   time   2 1260 360.517 1.55e-124     * 0.281



Assumption: Sphericity — variances of differences between all pairs of time points are equal.

title: Debugging Plots
text:
Debugging plots are essential tools for diagnosing issues in data visualization and analysis. They help identify problems such as incorrect data representation, scaling issues, or unexpected patterns in the data. In this guide, we will explore various techniques and tools for creating effective debugging plots.





Missing or incorrect data types
# Check data types
str(mtcars)

# Check for missing values
sum(is.na(mtcars))

# Visualize missing patterns
library(naniar)
vis_miss(mtcars)
Outliers affecting scales
# Check for outliers
boxplot(mtcars$mpg)

# Use robust statistics
library(robustbase)
summary(mtcars$mpg)





Mapping vs Setting Aesthetics
# Correct: Map color to variable
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point()

# Incorrect: Setting color globally
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = "red")  # This sets all points to red
Factor Level Issues
# Check factor levels
levels(mtcars$cyl)

# Reorder factors if needed
mtcars$cyl <- factor(mtcars$cyl, levels = c("4", "6", "8"))
Geom Conflicts
# Error: Can't use geom_bar with y aesthetic
# ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = value)) + geom_bar()

# Correct: Use stat = "identity"
ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = value)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "identity")







# Check ggplot object structure
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
str(p)

# View plot data
p$data
p$mapping



# Build plot incrementally
p1 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg))
print(p1)  # Should show empty plot

p2 <- p1 + geom_point()
print(p2)  # Check if points appear

p3 <- p2 + theme_minimal()
print(p3)  # Check theme application



# Enable ggplot2 debugging
options(ggplot2.debug = TRUE)

# Check for warnings
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()






# Problem: Length mismatch
# ggplot(data, aes(x = x_var, y = y_var, color = short_vector))

# Solution: Ensure vectors are same length or use single values
ggplot(data, aes(x = x_var, y = y_var, color = factor(category)))



# Problem: Wrong scale type
# ggplot(data, aes(x = factor_var, y = numeric_var)) + scale_x_continuous()

# Solution: Use appropriate scale
ggplot(data, aes(x = factor_var, y = numeric_var)) + scale_x_discrete()



# Problem: Typo in parameter name
# geom_point(size = 3)  # Correct
# geom_point(siz = 3)   # Incorrect

# Solution: Check documentation
?geom_point






# Residual plots for model diagnostics
model <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
plot(model)

# QQ plots for normality
qqnorm(mtcars$mpg)
qqline(mtcars$mpg)



# Correlation plots
library(corrplot)
corrplot(cor(mtcars))

# Pairs plots
pairs(mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "hp")])



# Plot data distributions
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg)) + 
  geom_histogram() + 
  facet_wrap(~ cyl)

# Check for data issues
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_text(aes(label = rownames(mtcars)), check_overlap = TRUE)






# When plot fails
tryCatch({
  ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
}, error = function(e) {
  print(e)
  traceback()
})



library(profvis)

# Profile plotting code
profvis({
  p <- ggplot(large_dataset, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point()
  print(p)
})



# Check memory usage
gc()

# For large datasets, use sampling
sample_data <- mtcars[sample(nrow(mtcars), 1000, replace = TRUE), ]
ggplot(sample_data, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()





Start simple: Build plots incrementally
Check data first: Validate input data before plotting
Use reproducible examples: Create minimal examples that reproduce issues
Read error messages carefully: They often point to the exact problem
Check package versions: Ensure compatible versions of ggplot2 and extensions
Use debugging tools: Leverage R’s debugging functions and ggplot2’s debug options
Document fixes: Keep notes on solutions for future reference

title: Plotting Tools
text:
This chapter introduces various tools and libraries available in R for creating visualizations. It covers base R plotting functions, as well as popular packages like ggplot2 and lattice, which offer advanced capabilities for creating complex and customizable plots.


R’s built-in plotting functions provide a solid foundation for data visualization:


# Scatter plot
plot(x = mtcars$wt, y = mtcars$mpg,
     xlab = "Weight", ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
     main = "Scatter Plot Example")

# Line plot
plot(x = 1:10, y = (1:10)^2, type = "l",
     xlab = "X", ylab = "Y^2")

# Bar plot
barplot(height = c(10, 15, 8, 12),
        names.arg = c("A", "B", "C", "D"))

# Histogram
hist(mtcars$mpg, breaks = 10,
     xlab = "Miles per Gallon",
     main = "Histogram of MPG")



# Multiple plots in one window
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))  # 2x2 grid

plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
hist(mtcars$mpg)
boxplot(mtcars$mpg ~ mtcars$cyl)
plot(density(mtcars$mpg))

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))  # Reset to single plot




ggplot2 is the most popular R package for data visualization, based on the Grammar of Graphics:


library(ggplot2)

# Basic scatter plot
ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point()

# Adding aesthetics
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "MPG vs Weight by Cylinders",
       x = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
       y = "Miles per Gallon")



# Points, lines, bars
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg))

p + geom_point()           # Scatter plot
p + geom_smooth()          # Smooth line
p + geom_line()            # Line plot
p + geom_bar(stat = "identity")  # Bar plot
p + geom_histogram()       # Histogram
p + geom_boxplot()         # Box plot



# Faceting
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ cyl) +
  theme_minimal()

# Custom themes
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("Custom Theme Example")




Lattice provides trellis graphics for multivariate data:
library(lattice)

# Scatter plot matrix
splom(mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "hp")])

# Conditional plots
xyplot(mpg ~ wt | factor(cyl), data = mtcars,
       layout = c(3, 1))

# 3D plots
cloud(mpg ~ wt * hp, data = mtcars)





library(plotly)

# Convert ggplot to interactive
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
ggplotly(p)

# Native plotly
plot_ly(mtcars, x = ~wt, y = ~mpg, type = "scatter", mode = "markers")



library(ggvis)

# Interactive ggplot2-like syntax
mtcars %>%
  ggvis(x = ~wt, y = ~mpg) %>%
  layer_points() %>%
  add_tooltip(function(df) paste("Weight:", df$wt, "MPG:", df$mpg))






library(ggstatsplot)

# Statistical plots with tests
ggbetweenstats(data = mtcars, x = cyl, y = mpg)



library(ggplot2)
library(maps)

# Basic map
world <- map_data("world")
ggplot(world, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = "lightblue", color = "black")



library(igraph)
library(ggraph)

# Create network
g <- make_ring(10)
ggraph(g, layout = "circle") +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point(size = 5)





Base R: Quick plots, statistical graphics
ggplot2: Publication-quality static plots, complex customizations
Lattice: Multivariate data, trellis displays
plotly/ggvis: Interactive web-based visualizations
Specialized packages: Domain-specific visualizations (maps, networks, etc.)





Know your data: Choose plot types that best represent your data
Keep it simple: Avoid clutter, focus on the message
Use color effectively: Consider colorblind-friendly palettes
Label clearly: Include informative titles, axis labels, legends
Test different tools: Experiment with different packages for the best result

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggstatsplot is an R package that combines statistical tests and publication-ready visualisations in a single function call. Each plot automatically selects, runs, and annotates the appropriate statistical test based on your data, displaying results directly on the figure.
This removes a common workflow bottleneck: running a test in one place, building a plot in another, and manually annotating results.

install.packages("ggstatsplot")
library(ggstatsplot)

Why use it?

One function produces both the visual and the statistical result
Automatically annotates effect sizes and confidence intervals
Sensible defaults — works out of the box for most common comparisons
Output is a ggplot2 object, so you can add layers or themes as usual

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggstatsplot is an R package that combines statistical tests and publication-ready visualisations in a single function call. Each plot automatically selects, runs, and annotates the appropriate statistical test based on your data, displaying results directly on the figure.
This removes a common workflow bottleneck: running a test in one place, building a plot in another, and manually annotating results.

install.packages("ggstatsplot")
library(ggstatsplot)

Why use it?

One function produces both the visual and the statistical result
Automatically annotates effect sizes and confidence intervals
Sensible defaults — works out of the box for most common comparisons
Output is a ggplot2 object, so you can add layers or themes as usual

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
section: Core functions covered in this module
text:
Core functions covered in this module



Function
Use case




ggbetweenstats()
Compare groups (independent samples)


ggscatterstats()
Correlation between two continuous variables


gghistostats()
Distribution of a single continuous variable

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggbetweenstats() — Group Comparisons
Use this when you want to compare a continuous variable across two or more independent groups.

library(ggstatsplot)

# Compare systolic BP across fuel type groups
ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = fuel_type,         # grouping variable (categorical)
  y     = sbp_0m,            # outcome variable (continuous)
  title = "Systolic BP by Fuel Type"
)

What the output shows:

A violin + boxplot combination with individual data points
The statistical test used (Welch’s ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis, chosen automatically)
The p-value, effect size (η² or ε²), and confidence interval
Pairwise comparisons (if more than 2 groups)

Choosing parametric vs non-parametric:

# Force non-parametric (Kruskal-Wallis)
ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = fuel_type,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  type  = "nonparametric"   # "parametric", "nonparametric", "robust", "bayes"
)

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggscatterstats() — Correlation
Use this when you want to examine the relationship between two continuous variables.

ggscatterstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = current_age,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  title = "Age vs Systolic BP at Baseline"
)

What the output shows:

A scatter plot with a linear trend line and confidence band
Pearson (or Spearman) correlation coefficient, r
p-value and 95% confidence interval for r
Marginal histograms on both axes

Using Spearman instead of Pearson:

ggscatterstats(
  data = overall_up,
  x    = current_age,
  y    = sbp_0m,
  type = "nonparametric"   # uses Spearman's rho
)

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
gghistostats() — Distribution
Use this when you want to visualise the distribution of a single continuous variable with a one-sample test.

gghistostats(
  data     = overall_up,
  x        = current_age,
  title    = "Distribution of Age at Enrolment",
  test.value = 40          # hypothesised population mean
)

What the output shows:

Histogram with overlaid density curve
One-sample t-test (or Wilcoxon signed-rank) against the specified test.value
Mean, median, and their confidence intervals

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
Reading the statistical annotation
Every ggstatsplot figure includes a subtitle with the test results in a standardised format:
Welch's ANOVA, F(2, 147.3) = 5.23, p = 0.006, ω² = 0.06, 95% CI [0.01, 0.14]



Component
Meaning




Test name
Which test was used (selected automatically)


Test statistic
F, t, χ², H etc.


p-value
Statistical significance


Effect size
Practical significance (ω², d, r, etc.)


95% CI
Uncertainty around the effect size









TipInterpreting effect sizes




η² / ω²: Small ≈ 0.01, Medium ≈ 0.06, Large ≈ 0.14 (for ANOVA)
Cohen’s d: Small ≈ 0.2, Medium ≈ 0.5, Large ≈ 0.8 (for t-tests)
r: Small ≈ 0.1, Medium ≈ 0.3, Large ≈ 0.5 (for correlation)

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
Quick reference

# Two-group comparison
ggbetweenstats(data = df, x = group, y = outcome)

# Correlation
ggscatterstats(data = df, x = var1, y = var2)

# Distribution
gghistostats(data = df, x = continuous_var, test.value = 0)

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Note



This module builds on Quarto Basics. It assumes you can create and render a .qmd file and write basic code chunks.

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
What you will learn

Parameterised reports — run the same document for different subgroups
Inline R code — embed values directly in prose
Cross-references for figures and tables
Multiple output formats from one source file
Integrating gtsummary tables in Quarto

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Parameterised Reports
Parameters let you run the same document with different inputs — for example, generating one report per hospital, intervention group, or region.

1. Declare parameters in the YAML header
---
title: "Site Report"
params:
  site_name: "Site A"
  intervention: "Control"
---


2. Use parameters in code

# params$site_name and params$intervention are available as R objects
site_data <- overall_up |>
  filter(site == params$site_name,
         intervention == params$intervention)

nrow(site_data)



3. Render with different parameter values

# Render from R for a specific site
quarto::quarto_render(
  input  = "site_report.qmd",
  output_file = "site_a_report.html",
  execute_params = list(
    site_name    = "Site A",
    intervention = "Intervention"
  )
)



4. Batch render — one file per site

library(purrr)

sites <- c("Site A", "Site B", "Site C")

walk(sites, \(site) {
  quarto::quarto_render(
    input          = "site_report.qmd",
    output_file    = paste0(tolower(gsub(" ", "_", site)), "_report.html"),
    execute_params = list(site_name = site)
  )
})

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Inline R Code
Embedding computed values directly in text avoids copy-paste errors and keeps your document reproducible.
Syntax:
200

# In a code chunk (runs silently):
n_total  <- nrow(overall_up)
mean_age <- round(mean(overall_up$current_age, na.rm = TRUE), 1)

In Quarto prose:
The study enrolled 200 participants with a mean age of
NA years (SD = 14.3).
Rendered output:

The study enrolled 1 248 participants with a mean age of 38.4 years (SD = 11.2).







Tip



Compute all summary values in one early code chunk marked #| include: false, then reference them via inline code throughout the document.

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Cross-References
Cross-references auto-number figures and tables and create clickable links.

Figures
Add a label that starts with fig- and a fig-cap:
```{r}
#| label: fig-sbp-hist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of baseline systolic blood pressure."
ggplot(overall_up, aes(x = sbp_0m)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(x = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", y = "Count")
```
Reference in text: @fig-sbp-hist → renders as “Figure 1”


Tables
Add a label starting with tbl- and a tbl-cap:
```{r}
#| label: tbl-demographics
#| tbl-cap: "Baseline characteristics of study participants."
library(gtsummary)
overall_up |>
  select(current_age, sex, tobacco_type, fuel_type) |>
  tbl_summary()
```
Reference in text: @tbl-demographics → renders as “Table 1”

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Multiple Output Formats
One .qmd file can produce HTML, PDF, and Word output.
---
title: "Study Report"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    theme: flatly
  pdf:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true
  docx:
    toc: true
---
Render all formats at once:
quarto render study_report.qmd






WarningPDF requirements



PDF rendering requires a LaTeX installation. Install tinytex from R:
install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()

title: Regression Interpretation Cheat Sheet
text:
Output
Reads as
Example (adjusted SBP model)




β (slope)
Change in mean outcome per 1-unit rise in x, others held constant — always give units
1.8 mmHg per g/day


Intercept
Mean outcome when all x = 0 — often meaningless (age 0?) so centre x
lm(sbp ~ I(age-50)): intercept = SBP at age 50


Categorical β
Difference vs the reference level
Men vs women: 3.8 mmHg


95% CI
Plausible values of the true β
1.2 to 2.4


p-value
Chance of data this extreme if true β = 0 — not effect size
< 0.001


R² / adj. R²
Share of variability accounted for (adjusted penalises extra terms)
0.39 / 0.37


Residual SE
Typical prediction miss, in outcome units
13.5 mmHg


CI vs PI
CI = mean of a group; PI = a new individual (wider)
predict(m, interval = "confidence" / "prediction")



Crude vs adjusted: crude salt β = 3.4 → adjusted 1.8 (a change ≥ 10% ⇒ confounding matters).











Assumption
Check
Violation looks like
Fix




Linearity
Residuals vs x (loess)
Curved line
Add x², spline, transform


Independence
Design; residuals by cluster; ICC
Clustered residuals
Mixed model, GEE, cluster-robust SE


Normal residuals
Q–Q plot
Points leave the line
Transform, bootstrap (matters for small n)


Equal variance
Residuals vs fitted; Breusch–Pagan
Funnel
Robust SE (vcovHC), transform


Multicollinearity
VIF (check_collinearity)
VIF > 5–10, β unstable
Keep one / combine



performance::check_model(m) · check_normality() · check_heteroscedasticity() · car::vif()




✅ Choose covariates from a DAG / theory, fix them before looking at p-values
✅ Report crude and adjusted; state the reference of every factor
⚠️ step() (AIC) = exploration only: biased β, narrow CIs, unstable
⛔ “Univariable p < 0.2 → in the model” can drop real confounders

title: Regression Interpretation Cheat Sheet
text:
2 · Logistic regression — reading the output

logit(p) = ln[ p / (1 − p) ] = β₀ + β₁x₁ + …   |   OR = e^β (one-unit change)   |   OR = 1 ⇔ β = 0









Output
Reads as
Example




β
Change in log-odds per 1-unit x
0.214


OR = exp(β)
Multiplies the odds by this factor per 1 unit; per k units: OR^k
OR 1.24 per g/day; per 5 g = 2.91


95% CI
Exponentiate the CI limits of β (so the CI is asymmetric on the OR scale)
1.11 – 1.39


OR > 1 / < 1
Higher / lower odds; CI containing 1 ⇒ not significant



Deviance
−2 × log-likelihood (relative to perfect); smaller = better
null 687 → 511


LR test
Compare nested models: 2×(logLik₁ − logLik₀) ~ χ²(df). Preferred to Wald for model comparison and multi-df terms
anova(m0, m1, test = "LRT"), lmtest::lrtest(), drop1(m, test="LRT")


AIC
−2 logLik + 2k; lower is better; works for non-nested (same rows!)
AIC(m1, m2)


Pseudo-R²
McFadden / Nagelkerke / Tjur — not % variance explained; run low; descriptive only
0.26 / 0.38 / 0.29


Calibration
Predicted risk ≈ observed risk? Plot deciles; Hosmer–Lemeshow (p > 0.05 OK, but low power/bin-dependent)
performance_hosmer(m)


Discrimination
AUC = P(random case ranked above random non-case): 0.5 chance · 0.7–0.8 ok · 0.8–0.9 good
AUC 0.82 (pROC::roc)




Common outcome? OR ≠ PR
Prevalence 32%. Age 50+ vs <50: OR 5.1 but PR 3.1. OR ≈ PR only if the outcome is rare (< ~10%). For “times as likely”: glm(family = poisson) + lmtest::coeftest(m, vcov. = sandwich::vcovHC(m, "HC0")), or log-binomial.


Write it up

Linear: “Each 1 g/day higher salt intake was associated with a 1.8 mmHg higher SBP (95% CI 1.2 to 2.4), adjusted for age, BMI, sex, residence, education, tobacco, alcohol and physical activity.”
Logistic: “Each 1 g/day higher salt intake was associated with 24% higher odds of hypertension (aOR 1.24; 95% CI 1.11–1.39).”



Pitfall checklist
☐ outcome type → model ☐ covariates pre-specified ☐ units + reference stated ☐ CI, not just p ☐ assumptions checked ☐ ≥ 10 events per variable ☐ clustering acknowledged ☐ OR not read as risk ☐ pseudo-R² ≠ R² ☐ association, not causation

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
text:
Where we are

Session 1: regression models the average outcome as a function of predictors
Today: the simplest case — one continuous predictor, one continuous outcome
By the end you can:

write and read the equation, in units
predict, and know when to use a confidence vs a prediction interval
explain residuals and OLS without calculus
report R² and adjusted R² sensibly
centre predictors so the intercept means something

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
text:
The equation

SBPi = β0 + β1 × salti + εi


β₀ (intercept) — average SBP when salt = 0
β₁ (slope) — change in average SBP for each 1-unit increase in salt (mmHg per g/day)
ε (error / residual) — everything else that makes person i differ from the line

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
text:
Fit it with lm()

m1 <- lm(sbp ~ salt_g, data = ncd)
summary(m1)


Call:
lm(formula = sbp ~ salt_g, data = ncd)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-41.857 -10.844  -0.434   9.888  55.093 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 107.4202     2.1490   49.98   <2e-16 ***
salt_g        3.3893     0.2801   12.10   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 15.14 on 580 degrees of freedom
  (18 observations deleted due to missingness)
Multiple R-squared:  0.2015,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.2001 
F-statistic: 146.4 on 1 and 580 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16



Read the Estimate column first. Then Std. Error, t, p. Then residual standard error and R². We will take each in turn today and in Session 3.

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
text:
Interpretation — always in units

Each extra 1 g/day of salt → mean SBP 3.4 mmHg higher


“mmHg per g/day” — the slope carries units of the outcome over units of the predictor
This is a crude estimate (no other variables yet) — Session 3 adjusts it
It describes an association across people, not what happens if one person changes their diet

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
section: The unit you choose changes the number
text:
The unit you choose changes the number

tibble(
  `Predictor unit`    = c("per 1 g/day", "per 5 g/day", "per 1 SD of salt"),
  `Change in SBP (mmHg)` = round(b1 * c(1, 5, sd(ncd$salt_g, na.rm = TRUE)), 1)
)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  `Predictor unit` `Change in SBP (mmHg)`
  <chr>                             <dbl>
1 per 1 g/day                         3.4
2 per 5 g/day                        16.9
3 per 1 SD of salt                    7.6



Same model, same data — three different-looking numbers. Always report the unit, and pick an increment that is clinically meaningful (5 g ≈ a teaspoon of salt).

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
text:
The intercept


No one in the survey eats 0 g of salt — the intercept is an extrapolation. Keep that in mind: we return to it under centering.

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
text:
Predict with predict()

new_salt <- tibble(salt_g = c(5, 8, 12))
predict(m1, newdata = new_salt)

       1        2        3 
124.3668 134.5349 148.0922 



“Adults who eat 8 g/day have a mean SBP of about 135 mmHg.”


Predict only within the range of the data (about 2–14 g/day). Beyond it, the straight line is a guess.

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
section: Two different questions, two different intervals
text:
Two different questions, two different intervals



Confidence interval
“What is the average SBP of all adults who eat 8 g/day?”
→ uncertainty about the line



Prediction interval
“What SBP might the next patient who eats 8 g/day have?”
→ line uncertainty plus person-to-person scatter

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
section: CI vs PI in R: interval =
text:
CI vs PI in R: interval =

predict(m1, new_salt, interval = "confidence") |> round(1)   # for the MEAN

    fit   lwr   upr
1 124.4 122.6 126.1
2 134.5 133.2 135.8
3 148.1 145.2 150.9

predict(m1, new_salt, interval = "prediction") |> round(1)   # for an INDIVIDUAL

    fit   lwr   upr
1 124.4  94.6 154.2
2 134.5 104.8 164.3
3 148.1 118.2 178.0



At 8 g/day: mean SBP 135 (95% CI 133–136) but an individual may lie anywhere from 105 to 164.

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
text:
Both bands on one plot

grid <- tibble(salt_g = seq(2, 14, length.out = 100))
ci <- predict(m1, grid, interval = "confidence") |> as_tibble() |> rename(ci_lwr = lwr, ci_upr = upr)
pi <- predict(m1, grid, interval = "prediction") |> as_tibble() |> select(pi_lwr = lwr, pi_upr = upr)

bind_cols(grid, ci, pi) |>
  ggplot(aes(salt_g)) +
  geom_point(data = ncd, aes(y = sbp), alpha = .25, colour = col_blue) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = pi_lwr, ymax = pi_upr), fill = col_blue, alpha = .15) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ci_lwr, ymax = ci_upr), fill = col_red, alpha = .5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit), colour = col_navy, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Salt intake (g/day)", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)",
       caption = "Red = 95% CI for the mean · Blue = 95% prediction interval for an individual")



Notice the CI band is narrowest near the mean of salt and flares at the ends. The PI band is wide everywhere and contains roughly 95% of the dots.

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
text: Both bands on one plot

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
text:
Fitted values and residuals

Fitted value ŷ = what the line predicts for a person. Residual = observed − fitted.


augment(m1) |> select(sbp, salt_g, .fitted, .resid) |> head(5) |> mutate(across(everything(), ~ round(.x, 1)))

# A tibble: 5 × 4
    sbp salt_g .fitted .resid
  <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>
1   131    6.9    131.    0.2
2   135    9      138.   -2.9
3   127    5.8    127.   -0.1
4   155   10.2    142    13  
5   138    6.3    129.    9.2

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
section: OLS: choose the line with the smallest squared misses
text:
OLS: choose the line with the smallest squared misses


Each red square has side = the size of the residual; its area is the squared residual. OLS finds the intercept and slope that make the total red area as small as possible. No calculus needed: R does the minimisation. Axes are standardised only so the squares look square.

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
text:
Residuals vs fitted: first look

augment(m1) |>
  ggplot(aes(.fitted, .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .4, colour = col_blue) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = col_red) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, colour = col_navy, method = "loess", formula = y ~ x) +
  labs(x = "Fitted SBP (mmHg)", y = "Residual (mmHg)")



Residuals should scatter evenly around 0. Hold that thought — Session 4 reads this plot properly.

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
section: R²: how much of the variation does the model account for?
text:
R²: how much of the variation does the model account for?

r2(m1)

# R2 for Linear Regression
       R2: 0.202
  adj. R2: 0.200

sigma(m1)   # residual standard error, in mmHg

[1] 15.13919



R² = 0.2 → salt alone accounts for about 20% of the variation in SBP
Residual SE ≈ 15 mmHg: a typical miss — it is why the prediction interval is so wide

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
section: R² always rises; adjusted R² punishes junk
text:
R² always rises; adjusted R² punishes junk

set.seed(2026)
junk <- as_tibble(matrix(rnorm(nrow(ncd) * 20), ncol = 20, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("z", 1:20))))
d_j  <- bind_cols(ncd |> select(sbp, salt_g), junk) |> drop_na()

map_dfr(c(0, 5, 20), \(k) {
  f <- reformulate(c("salt_g", head(names(junk), k)), "sbp")
  s <- summary(lm(f, data = d_j))
  tibble(`random noise variables added` = k, R2 = round(s$r.squared, 3), `adjusted R2` = round(s$adj.r.squared, 3))
})

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  `random noise variables added`    R2 `adjusted R2`
                           <dbl> <dbl>         <dbl>
1                              0 0.202         0.2  
2                              5 0.21          0.201
3                             20 0.227         0.198



Adding pure noise raises R² every time; adjusted R² charges for each extra parameter. Use adjusted R² when you compare models of different size.

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
text:
Reading R² sensibly



A low R² does not mean the predictor is unimportant
BP depends on age, genes, diet, stress… A salt slope can be real and clinically important with R² of 0.2.



A high R² does not mean the model is right
A model can fit well and still violate assumptions, or fit this dataset only (overfitting). R² says nothing about causation.

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
text:
An intercept at age 0?

m_age <- lm(sbp ~ age, data = ncd)
coef(m_age)

(Intercept)         age 
 96.3162078   0.7430034 



The intercept says: a 0-year-old has SBP 96 mmHg. Our sample is aged 30–69, so this describes nobody.

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
section: Centering: move the zero to a meaningful place
text:
Centering: move the zero to a meaningful place

ncd <- ncd |> mutate(age_c = age - 50)          # 0 now means "age 50"
m_age_c <- lm(sbp ~ age_c, data = ncd)

bind_rows(raw = tidy(m_age), centred = tidy(m_age_c), .id = "model") |>
  select(model, term, estimate) |> mutate(estimate = round(estimate, 2))

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  model   term        estimate
  <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
1 raw     (Intercept)    96.3 
2 raw     age             0.74
3 centred (Intercept)   133.  
4 centred age_c           0.74



Slope unchanged (0.74 mmHg per year)
Intercept now = expected SBP at age 50 = 133 mmHg → interpretable
Centre on the mean or on a clinically meaningful value (age 50, BMI 25)

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
text: Same line, new origin

title: Session 2 — Simple Linear Regression
section: Scaling: change the unit, not the relationship
text:
Scaling: change the unit, not the relationship

tidy(lm(sbp ~ I(age / 10), data = ncd)) |> select(term, estimate) |> mutate(estimate = round(estimate, 2))   # per 10 years

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  term        estimate
  <chr>          <dbl>
1 (Intercept)    96.3 
2 I(age/10)       7.43

tidy(lm(sbp ~ scale(age), data = ncd))  |> select(term, estimate) |> mutate(estimate = round(estimate, 2))   # per 1 SD

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  term        estimate

Score and take-home
Your score: 

Slope = change in mean outcome per 1 predictor unit — always say the units
CI → the mean; PI → an individual (always wider)
OLS minimises the sum of squared residuals
R² is descriptive; use adjusted R² to compare sizes; low R² ≠ unimportant

title: Session 4 — Assumptions of Linear Regression
text:
Where we are

We have a model: sbp ~ salt_g + age + bmi + sex + residence + education + tobacco + alcohol + phys_act
Its p-values and CIs are only trustworthy if its assumptions are reasonable
For each assumption today: what it means → how to check → what a violation looks like in OUR data → what to do

title: Session 4 — Assumptions of Linear Regression
text:
The checklist









Assumption
Plain meaning




L
Linearity
The mean outcome changes in a straight line with each predictor


I
Independence
One person’s error tells you nothing about another’s


N
Normality of residuals
Residuals are roughly bell-shaped


E
Equal variance (homoscedasticity)
Spread of residuals is the same at every fitted value


M
No severe multicollinearity
Predictors are not near-copies of each other




Plus a look for influential points (a few people driving the result).

title: Session 4 — Assumptions of Linear Regression
section: What goes wrong when each fails
text:
What goes wrong when each fails







Violation
Main consequence




Non-linearity
Biased β — the line is the wrong shape


Non-independence (clusters)
SEs too small → CIs too narrow, p too small


Non-normal residuals
Usually minor if n is large; matters for small n and prediction intervals


Unequal variance
SEs wrong (usually too small/large in places); estimates less efficient


Multicollinearity
SEs inflated, β unstable, even sign flips

title: Session 4 — Assumptions of Linear Regression
text:
The one-page panel: check_model()

check_model(m, check = c("linearity", "homogeneity", "qq", "outliers"))



Walk through the four panels. Top-left reference line should be flat and horizontal; it curves. Top-right should be flat; it rises (funnel). Q-Q points should sit on the line; they roughly do. Bottom-right should keep points inside the contour lines. We now take each assumption in turn.

title: Session 4 — Assumptions of Linear Regression
text:
Linearity: what and how


Means: each continuous predictor has a straight-line relationship with the mean outcome.
Check: plot residuals vs each continuous predictor (and vs fitted) with a smooth curve — it should be flat.


Violation looks like: a curved (U, ∩ or banana-shaped) smooth line in the residual plot.

title: Session 4 — Assumptions of Linear Regression
section: In our data: age is slightly curved
text:
In our data: age is slightly curved

cc |>
  mutate(res = resid(m)) |>
  ggplot(aes(age, res)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3, colour = col_blue) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = col_red, formula = y ~ x) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Residual (mmHg)")



Residuals are slightly negative in the middle and positive at the ends: SBP rises faster at older ages than a straight line allows. A formal check: resettest().

resettest(m, power = 2, type = "regressor")

A small p-value suggests curvature somewhere — but look at the plot to see where and how much.

text:
What to do about non-linearity

m_quad <- lm(sbp ~ salt_g + age + I(age^2) + bmi + sex + residence + education +
               tobacco + alcohol + phys_act, data = cc)
anova(m, m_quad)

Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: sbp ~ salt_g + age + bmi + sex + residence + education + tobacco + 
    alcohol + phys_act
Model 2: sbp ~ salt_g + age + I(age^2) + bmi + sex + residence + education + 
    tobacco + alcohol + phys_act
  Res.Df   RSS Df Sum of Sq      F  Pr(>F)  
1    538 98422                              
2    537 97336  1    1085.6 5.9891 0.01471 *
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



Add a squared term (I(age^2)) — the improvement is significant
Better still for flexible shapes: splines (splines::ns(), mgcv) — mentioned in Session 6
Or categorise (age bands) — simple but throws information away
Or transform the predictor (e.g. log) when the curve is monotonic

title: Session 4 — Assumptions of Linear Regression
text:
Independence: what and how


Means: the residual of one person carries no information about another’s.
Typically violated by: people in the same village / household / clinic, repeated measures on the same person, time series.

Check: by design first (how were people sampled?), then plot residuals by cluster and estimate the intraclass correlation.

section: In our data: people are clustered in 20 villages
text:

cc |>
  mutate(res = resid(m)) |>
  ggplot(aes(reorder(village, res, FUN = median), res)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#d6eaf8") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = col_red) +
  labs(x = "Village (ordered by median residual)", y = "Residual (mmHg)") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = .5))

title: Session 4 — Assumptions of Linear Regression
text:
How big is the clustering?

a   <- anova(lm(resid(m) ~ factor(cc$village)))
msb <- a$`Mean Sq`[1]; msw <- a$`Mean Sq`[2]; k <- mean(table(cc$village))
icc <- (msb - msw) / (msb + (k - 1) * msw)
c(ICC = round(icc, 3), design_effect = round(1 + (k - 1) * icc, 2))

          ICC design_effect 
        0.058         2.530 



ICC ≈ 0.06: about 6% of the residual variation lies between villages
Design effect ≈ 2.5: for village-level exposures the standard errors may be too small by about √2.5 ≈ 1.6×

title: Session 4 — Assumptions of Linear Regression
text:
What to do about non-independence

In this workshop we only detect and discuss the village clustering — we do not model it.


Mixed models with a random intercept per village (lme4)
GEE (geepack) or cluster-robust standard errors
Survey-design methods for complex samples such as NFHS (survey)
At minimum: report the design, state the limitation, and be cautious with village-level predictors (e.g., residence)

title: Session 4 — Assumptions of Linear Regression
section: Normality of residuals: what and how
text:
Normality of residuals: what and how


Means: the residuals (not the outcome!) are roughly bell-shaped.
Check: Q–Q plot — points should follow the diagonal; a histogram; tests are secondary.


With n ≈ 550, the central limit theorem protects CIs for β. Normality matters most for small samples and prediction intervals.

augment(m) |>

  stat_qq(alpha = .5, colour = col_blue) + stat_qq_line(colour = col_red, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Standardised residuals")



check_normality(m)

OK: residuals appear as normally distributed (p = 0.882).

title: Session 4 — Assumptions of Linear Regression
text:
If normality is badly violated

Check for outliers or data errors first
Transform the outcome (e.g., log(sbp)) — then interpret as % change
Bootstrap the CIs (no normality assumption)
Robust regression (MASS::rlm) or a different model for the outcome type

title: Session 4 — Assumptions of Linear Regression
text:
Homoscedasticity: what and how


Means: the spread of residuals is the same at every fitted value.
Check: residuals vs fitted — a funnel (fan) shape means variance grows with the mean. Breusch–Pagan test.


Biological outcomes often get more variable at higher levels: older adults vary more in BP.

title: Session 4 — Assumptions of Linear Regression
text:
Tests for non-constant variance

check_heteroscedasticity(m)

Warning: Heteroscedasticity (non-constant error variance) detected (p < .001).

bptest(m)


    studentized Breusch-Pagan test

data:  m
BP = 22.89, df = 12, p-value = 0.02867



Both flag non-constant variance. They are variants of the Breusch–Pagan test (the second is the studentised, more robust version), so their p-values differ slightly — name the test you used. The effect is mild: residual SD roughly 12 mmHg under 45 vs 15 mmHg at 55+.

title: Session 4 — Assumptions of Linear Regression
section: What to do about unequal variance
text:
What to do about unequal variance

rob <- coeftest(m, vcov. = sandwich::vcovHC(m, type = "HC3"))
tibble(term = names(coef(m)),
       SE_usual  = round(summary(m)$coefficients[, 2], 3),
       SE_robust = round(rob[, 2], 3)) |> filter(term %in% c("salt_g", "age", "bmi", "sexMale"))

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  term    SE_usual SE_robust
  <chr>      <dbl>     <dbl>
1 salt_g     0.302     0.3  
2 age        0.062     0.062
3 bmi        0.182     0.173
4 sexMale    1.29      1.30 



Robust (sandwich) SEs: same β, honest SEs — the easiest fix (sandwich::vcovHC)
Transform the outcome (e.g., log(sbp)) or use weighted least squares
Our violation is mild: conclusions do not change — but you should know and say so

title: Session 4 — Assumptions of Linear Regression
text:
Multicollinearity: what and how


Means: two or more predictors carry nearly the same information, so the model cannot tell their effects apart.
Check: correlation matrix and VIF.


VIF = how much a coefficient’s variance is inflated by correlation with the other predictors.
Rule of thumb: > 5 worry, > 10 serious.

section: What collinearity does to the estimates
text:
What collinearity does to the estimates

m_bmi <- lm(sbp ~ salt_g + age + bmi, data = cc)
bind_rows(`BMI alone` = tidy(m_bmi), `BMI + waist` = tidy(m_both), .id = "model") |>
  filter(term == "bmi") |> select(model, estimate, std.error, p.value) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 3)))

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  model       estimate std.error    p.value
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>
1 BMI alone      0.814     0.182 0.00000957
2 BMI + waist   -0.537     0.528 0.31      




With waist added, the BMI coefficient shrinks toward zero (and can flip sign) while its SE roughly triples — each variable “steals” the other’s effect.

title: Session 4 — Assumptions of Linear Regression
text:
How to handle collinearity

Choose one on clinical grounds (BMI for an exposure of interest; waist if central adiposity is the question) — our fix
Combine into one measure (e.g., a ratio or first principal component)
Centre predictors if the collinearity comes from polynomial or interaction terms
Penalised regression (ridge/lasso — glmnet) when many correlated predictors
Do not drop by p-value alone

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
text:
Results sentence — linear regression

“After adjusting for age, BMI, sex, residence, education, tobacco, alcohol and physical activity, each 1 g/day higher salt intake was associated with a 1.8 mmHg higher systolic blood pressure (95% CI 1.2 to 2.4; p < 0.001) (n = 551; adjusted R² = 0.37).”


✔ Direction + size + units · ✔ CI · ✔ adjustment set · ✔ n · ✔ “associated with”
Give the crude estimate too (3.4 mmHg) so readers see the effect of adjustment

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
text:
Results sentence — logistic regression

“Hypertension was present in 32% of participants. After adjustment, each 1 g/day higher salt intake was associated with 24% higher odds of hypertension (adjusted OR 1.24; 95% CI 1.11 to 1.39). The model showed good discrimination (AUC 0.82).”


✔ Say “odds” (not risk) · ✔ unit of x · ✔ reference categories for categorical ORs
With a common outcome, add the prevalence ratio if you want to say “times as likely”

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
section: Tables and figures: what a reader needs
text:
Tables and figures: what a reader needs



Include

Units in row labels (per g/day, per 5 kg/m²)
Reference category for every categorical variable
n analysed (note missing data handling)
95% CI (not only p)
Footnote: adjustment set, abbreviations, model type




Avoid

“p = 0.000” (write p < 0.001)
Stars-only tables
Reporting β without the outcome units
Hiding the crude estimates

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
text:
The Methods paragraph

Model and why — “multiple linear regression for SBP; logistic regression for hypertension (SBP ≥ 140 or DBP ≥ 90)”
Covariates and rationale — “chosen a priori from a causal diagram/literature, not by automated selection”
Assumption checks — linearity, independence (clustering by village), residual normality, equal variance, collinearity (VIF); and how violations were handled
Missing data — “complete-case analysis; n = …”
Model assessment (logistic) — likelihood ratio tests, AIC, calibration, AUC
Software — R version and packages (below)

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
section: Software line: let R tell you
text:
Software line: let R tell you

R.version.string

[1] "R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24 ucrt)"

sapply(c("tidyverse", "gtsummary", "broom", "performance", "pROC", "car", "lmtest"),
       \(p) as.character(packageVersion(p)))

  tidyverse   gtsummary       broom performance        pROC         car 
    "2.0.0"     "2.5.1"    "1.0.13"    "0.17.1"    "1.19.1"     "3.1.5" 
     lmtest 
   "0.9.40" 



“Analyses were done in R 4.6.1 using the tidyverse, gtsummary, performance, car, lmtest and pROC packages.” Follow STROBE for observational studies.

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
section: Pitfall 1 — Stepwise selection presented as the analysis
text:
Pitfall 1 — Stepwise selection presented as the analysis

“Variables were selected by backward stepwise regression (AIC).” → biased β, narrow CIs, unstable model, ignores confounding logic.


Instead: pre-specify covariates from a DAG or the literature; report the same model whatever the p-values. If you use step(), label it exploratory (Session 3 demos).

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
text:
Pitfall 2 — “p < 0.2 into the model”

vars <- c("salt_g", "age", "bmi", "sex", "residence", "education", "tobacco", "alcohol", "phys_act")
p_uni <- map_dbl(vars, \(v) anova(glm(reformulate(v, "htn"), binomial, cc), test = "LRT")$`Pr(>Chi)`[2])
or_adj <- tidy(m_log, exponentiate = TRUE) |> filter(term %in% c("phys_actmoderate", "phys_acthigh", "residenceRural"))
tibble(variable = vars, `univariable p` = signif(p_uni, 2)) |> filter(variable %in% c("phys_act", "residence", "salt_g"))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  variable  `univariable p`
  <chr>               <dbl>
1 salt_g            4.9e-17
2 residence         8.8e- 1
3 phys_act          1  e+ 0

or_adj |> select(term, `adjusted OR` = estimate, p.value) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 2)))

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  term             `adjusted OR` p.value
  <chr>                    <dbl>   <dbl>
1 residenceRural            1.1    0.7  
2 phys_actmoderate          0.71   0.23 
3 phys_acthigh              0.57   0.041




Physical activity has univariable p ≈ 1 — a “p < 0.2” screen would drop it — yet adjusted for age, BMI and sex, high activity has OR ≈ 0.57. Confounding hides it from the crude test.

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
text:
Pitfalls 3–6: say it properly








Pitfall
✘ Don’t
✔ Do




3. β without units or reference
“Salt β = 1.8; sex β = 3.8”
“1.8 mmHg higher SBP per 1 g/day; men 3.8 mmHg higher than women (reference)”


4. OR read as risk
“50+ y are 5.1 times as likely to be hypertensive” (outcome 32%)
“…had 5.1 times the odds (PR 3.1)”


5. Pseudo-R² as R²
“The model explains 29% of the variance in hypertension”
“Tjur’s R² was 0.29 (a descriptive pseudo-R²)”


6. Statistical = clinical
“Highly significant (p < 0.001), therefore important”
“A 1.8 mmHg difference per g/day (95% CI 1.2–2.4): a 5 g reduction ≈ 9 mmHg lower mean SBP”

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
section: Pitfall 7 — Overfitting: too few events per variable
text:
Pitfall 7 — Overfitting: too few events per variable

events <- sum(cc$htn); params <- length(coef(m_log)) - 1
c(events = events, parameters = params, events_per_variable = round(events / params, 1))

             events          parameters events_per_variable 
              174.0                12.0                14.5 



Rule of thumb: ≥ 10 events per variable (events = the smaller outcome group); our model has 14.5 — acceptable
Too many predictors → the model memorises noise: great on this sample, poor on the next

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
text:
Overfitting in action: 60 pure-noise predictors

set.seed(3)
noise <- as_tibble(matrix(rnorm(nrow(cc) * 60), ncol = 60)); d_o <- bind_cols(htn = cc$htn, noise)
train <- sample(nrow(d_o), 300)
g_o <- glm(htn ~ ., binomial, d_o[train, ])
auc_in  <- auc(roc(d_o$htn[train],  fitted(g_o), quiet = TRUE))
auc_out <- auc(roc(d_o$htn[-train], predict(g_o, d_o[-train, ], type = "response"), quiet = TRUE))
round(c(AUC_on_training_data = as.numeric(auc_in), AUC_on_new_data = as.numeric(auc_out)), 2)

AUC_on_training_data      AUC_on_new_data 
                0.75                 0.58 



Pure noise can look “good” on the data that built it (AUC well above 0.5) and falls back toward 0.5 on new data — the signature of overfitting.

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
text:
Pitfall 8 — Ignoring assumptions and clustering

se_naive   <- summary(m_lin)$coefficients[, "Std. Error"]
se_cluster <- sqrt(diag(sandwich::vcovCL(m_lin, cluster = cc$village)))
tibble(term = names(se_naive), naive_SE = round(se_naive, 2), village_robust_SE = round(se_cluster, 2),
       ratio = round(se_cluster / se_naive, 2)) |> filter(term %in% c("salt_g", "age", "residenceRural"))

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  term           naive_SE village_robust_SE ratio
  <chr>             <dbl>             <dbl> <dbl>
1 salt_g             0.3               0.29  0.97
2 age                0.06              0.06  0.95
3 residenceRural     1.36              1.84  1.35



For village-level predictors (residence) the true SE is noticeably larger than the naive SE — naive CIs are too narrow
Individual-level predictors (salt) are less affected here, but you should still state the design and check assumptions
Remedies: mixed models, GEE, cluster-robust SE, survey methods (next slides)

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
text:
Pitfall 9 — Calling associations causal




“Salt causes hypertension (β = 1.8)”
“Tobacco increases SBP by 3 mmHg”





“Higher salt intake was associated with higher SBP”
“Tobacco users had 3 mmHg higher mean SBP”




A cross-sectional survey cannot establish temporal order
Adjustment handles measured confounders only; the DAG states your assumptions
Causal claims need design (RCT, strong quasi-experiment) and explicit causal reasoning

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
text:
Before you submit



Outcome type matches the model
Covariates pre-specified, with rationale
Crude and adjusted estimates
Units and reference categories
CIs, not just p



Assumptions checked and reported
Events per variable adequate
Clustering / design acknowledged
OR vs PR considered for common outcomes
Language: association, not causation

Model

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
text:
Take-home messages of the day

Outcome type → model; regression gives effects in units, with CIs
Confounding is why we adjust: crude ≠ adjusted
Choose covariates from theory, not from stepwise or p-values
Check assumptions — and say what you did about violations
Logistic: exp(β) = OR; assess with likelihood, calibration and discrimination; mind OR vs PR
Report like a scientist: units, references, CIs, limitations — and association ≠ causation

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (1/6)

Which sentence reports a linear regression result correctly?

Salt had a statistically significant effect on SBP in this sample of adults (p < 0.001)
Each extra g/day of salt went with 1.8 mmHg higher SBP (95% CI 1.2–2.4), adjusted
The salt β was 1.8 with p < 0.001, so salt is a strong determinant of blood pressure
Salt explained 1.8% of the variance in blood pressure after adjusting for other factors

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (2/6)

Why is ‘keep variables with univariable p < 0.2’ a poor strategy?

It retains too few variables to build a model that is useful for prediction
A variable can look unrelated alone but matter after adjusting for others
It leads to overfitting in every dataset, whatever the sample size may be
Univariable p-values cannot be calculated for a single predictor variable

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (3/6)

A cross-sectional survey finds higher salt intake is associated with higher SBP. Which conclusion is appropriate?

Salt intake causes hypertension in this whole community
Cutting salt will lower SBP by the coefficient amount in each person
Higher salt intake went with higher SBP; causation is unproven
No association exists because the R² is only moderate

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (4/6)

Using at least 10 events per variable, about how many predictors (counting every dummy variable) can a logistic model with 60 events support? (number)

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (5/6)

Participants in our survey come from 20 villages and resemble others in the same village. What feature of the design makes ordinary SEs too small for village-level predictors? (one word)

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (6/6)

Prevalence is 50% in adults aged 50+ and 16% in younger adults. What is the prevalence ratio? (1 decimal)

title: Session 6 — Interpreting and Reporting
text:
Score and close
Your score: 

You now have a workflow: look → model → check → compare → report
Re-run the labs on your own data; keep the cheat sheet beside you
Keep the pitfalls list beside your thesis draft

Thank you — questions?

title: Post-test · Show your growth
text:
Same skills as the pre-test, different questions. After submitting you will see your gain compared with your baseline.



Each TB patient ends as cured, failed, died or lost to follow-up (four unordered categories). Which family suits this outcome?

Ordinal logistic regression
Poisson regression for counts
Ordinary least-squares linear regression
Multinomial logistic regression



In a model for haemoglobin (g/dL), a household wealth score has β = 0.15. Which statement is correct?

Mean Hb is 0.15 g/dL higher per extra wealth unit, others fixed
Wealth explains 0.15 of the variance in haemoglobin
Each woman’s Hb rises 0.15 if her wealth score rises 1
Hb is 0.15 percent higher for each extra wealth unit in the sample



The residual SD is 20 mmHg. About how many mmHg is the half-width of a 95% prediction interval for one new patient? (whole number)


Adjusted R² is preferred to R² when comparing models of different size because it…

is unaffected by the number of observations used
measures how well the model predicts a new sample
always returns a value that is higher than plain R² itself
charges a penalty for each extra parameter in the model



Age is centred at 40 years before fitting. In the centred model the slope for age…

is smaller because the ages are now smaller
now describes the outcome at the age of 40 years alone
must be re-estimated as a percentage change
is identical to the slope from the uncentred model



The crude β of alcohol on SBP is +6; adjusted for sex it is +2. The most sensible reading is that…

sex is a mediator, so adjusting for it is a mistake
the sex-adjusted model contains a calculation error somewhere
sex confounds the association and explains much of the slope
alcohol has no real effect once sex is included in the model



With no schooling as the reference, primary = −1.0 and graduate = −3.0 mmHg. How many mmHg lower is graduate than primary? (1 decimal)


Which practice best protects against bias when choosing covariates?

Keep whichever variables are significant on their own
Pre-specify them from a causal diagram before seeing results
Add all available variables to maximise R-squared
Let stepwise selection decide and report the final model alone



BMI and waist circumference correlate at r = 0.95 and both enter a model. Which problem should you expect?

Non-independence of the observations collected
Inflated standard errors and unstable coefficients
Residuals that clearly fail the normality assumption
A curved relationship with the outcome variable



Disease prevalence is 40%. What are the odds of disease? (2 decimals)


The adjusted OR for high versus low activity is 0.55 (95% CI 0.33–0.95). Which wording is correct?

The CI lower limit is below 1, so it is not significant
Activity prevents 45% of cases in this population
High-activity adults were 45% less likely overall
High-activity adults had 45% lower odds, adjusted



Flag every flawed sentence from this results paragraph (cross-sectional study, 40% prevalence).

Rural residents had 1.8 times the odds of anaemia (95% CI 1.2–2.7).
So rural residents were 1.8 times as likely to be anaemic.
Each additional year of schooling was associated with 0.12 g/dL higher Hb (95% CI 0.05–0.19).
The model explains 31% of the variance in anaemia (McFadden R² = 0.31).
Wealth was kept because stepwise selection retained it.
Age had β = 0.04.

title: Dungeons & Dataframes — Roadmap
text:
Goal: turn the one-day Theory of Regression Analysis workshop into a game for learning medical statistics in R (Dungeons & Dataframes): a self-paced, gamified, tested environment for community-medicine residents and faculty. The platform is organised into tracks; Track 1 is Regression (the worlds in §3), and further tracks follow (§1.1). Within Regression, a learner goes from “I can run lm()” to “I can plan, run, check and report the right regression for my thesis”, and on into the models the workshop only names.
Scope decisions (v3):

Platform = medical statistics in R; regression is its first track. Name: Dungeons & Dataframes (deliberately not regression-specific). Worlds can be presented as dungeons.
R basics are a prerequisite. Learners are assumed to have basic-to-moderate R (import data, tidyverse verbs, simple plots, run a model and read summary()); a short readiness check (§2.3) advises anyone who is not ready (it points to the repo’s existing R Foundations track).
English only. It is a coding place; no translation work is planned.
Certificate: later. Completion certificates are a later-phase priority (Phase 6, with accounts and server verification).
Reviewer: content and statistics are reviewed by the author (community-medicine faculty); an optional external statistician check can be added before wide release.
Hosting: static now, accounts later. R practice: hybrid (§7).

The full site design (information architecture, game modes, skill tree, hybrid R labs, state model) is in Site design.







Principle
What it means in practice




Learning first, game second
Points reward understanding (first-try accuracy, no hints), never time spent or guessing.


Test what matters
Interpretation, judgement and error-spotting beat function recall. No “which function does X?” items.


Honest assessment
No giveaways: balanced option lengths, no “all of the above”, shuffled display, no key-first markup, explanations only after an attempt. Enforced by a linter in CI.


Real public-health context
Indian community-medicine scenarios and datasets (NCD survey, TB cohort, dengue counts, NFHS-type surveys).


Depth over breadth, track by track
No detours into general R teaching; each track goes deep (Track 1: modelling, interpretation, checking and reporting) before the next opens.


Three ways to practise
Quests (guided path), Case files (realistic thesis scenarios with decisions), Arcade (short repeatable drills): so mastery comes from varied retrieval, not one pass.


Real R, hybrid
Learners also run real R on the project datasets; the game checks results through verifiable codes (no server needed), with in-browser R as an optional later mode.


Works anywhere
Static files, offline-capable, no login needed for the core path; optional server features come later.


Evidence of gain
Every learner gets a baseline (pre-test) and a parallel post-test; the project measures learning gain, not just completion.


Reproducible content
One source of truth per item and per lab; everything built and verified by scripts.



Non-goals (for now): replacing a biostatistician, covering every statistical method in the first release, teaching R itself, translations, high-stakes certification (that needs proctoring and a server).



The skill tree and engine are track-agnostic: a track is a set of worlds, skills, items, case files and arcade games.








Track
Focus
Status




1 · Regression
Linear, logistic, counts, survival, clusters, surveys, missing data, prediction, causal (Worlds 1–16, §3)
✅ started (Worlds 1–2 playable)


2 · Comparing groups
t-tests, non-parametric tests, chi-square/Fisher, ANOVA, choosing a test, multiple testing, effect sizes
⬜ planned


3 · Epidemiological measures
Risk/odds/rate ratios, attributable fractions, standardisation, confounding by stratification (Mantel–Haenszel), screening metrics
⬜ planned


4 · Study design & sample size
Sampling, power and precision, randomisation, bias catalogue, cluster designs, reporting standards
⬜ planned


5 · Survey & health-systems analytics
Complex surveys, weights, small-area rates, time series for surveillance
⬜ planned


6 · Evidence synthesis & diagnostics
Meta-analysis, heterogeneity, diagnostic accuracy, decision curves
⬜ planned


7 · Reproducible reporting
Quarto, tables/figures, STROBE/CONSORT, thesis workflow
⬜ planned



Tracks unlock independently after the readiness check; a learner can start in any track whose prerequisite skills they hold.

title: Dungeons & Dataframes — Roadmap
text:
2. Audience and learning outcomes

2.1 Personas








Persona
Needs
Path




Resident writing a thesis
Right model, correct interpretation, reviewer-proof write-up
Core worlds 1–6, then 10, 11, 13, capstone

Concepts behind the code
Readiness check, pre-test, then skip to weak skills


Facilitator
Run a cohort, see who is stuck
Cohort mode and instructor dashboard (Phase 6)





2.2 Programme-level outcomes (ILOs)
After the full path a learner can:

Choose a regression family from the outcome type and study design, and justify it.
Fit and interpret linear, logistic, count, ordinal/nominal and survival models in units, with CIs.
Adjust for confounding using causal reasoning (DAGs) rather than significance filtering.
Diagnose and respond to violations (linearity, independence, variance, normality, collinearity, influence, proportional hazards).
Evaluate models (likelihood ratio, AIC, calibration, discrimination, validation).
Handle real-data problems: clustering, complex survey design, missing data, non-linearity, interaction.
Report to publication standards (STROBE/TRIPOD, units, reference categories, honest language).
Critique published analyses and avoid the nine standard pitfalls.

Outcomes are mapped to Bloom levels (remember → evaluate) per world in §3 and drive the item mix in §6.


2.3 Prerequisites and the readiness check
Assumed: basic-to-moderate R: projects/scripts, read_csv, dplyr verbs (filter, mutate, group/summarise), factors, ggplot2 basics, running lm()/glm() and printing summary(). Not assumed: any regression theory.
Readiness check (≈ 10 minutes, ungraded): 8 short items (reading a mutate/summarise pipeline, spotting a factor-level problem, interpreting a plot, reading a summary() table) plus 2 hands-on R tasks. Outcome: Ready → straight to the pre-test; Nearly → a 5-item brush-up list of skills plus links to the existing R Foundations pages; Not yet → R Foundations first. The check never blocks anyone: it advises.

title: Dungeons & Dataframes — Roadmap
text:
5. Gamification design

5.1 XP economy







Element
Rule




Base XP
Difficulty ★ = 10, ★★ = 20, ★★★ = 30


Attempt factor
First try ×1, second ×0.5, later ×0.25


Hints
Tiered (−3, −5, −8 XP); a world’s hints never reveal the answer text


Show answer
0 XP (never punished beyond that)


Boss
+50 XP bonus


Streak
Daily; bonus badges at 3 and 7 days; no XP for streak itself (avoids grinding)


Cap
An item pays out once (re-solving gives nothing)





5.2 Ranks
Field Volunteer (0) → Health Worker (100) → Medical Officer (250) → Epidemiologist (500) → Senior Epidemiologist (900) → Chief Biostatistician (1500). Thresholds are retuned from pilot data so a median learner reaches Epidemiologist by the end of World 6.


5.3 Badge catalogue (rules are data in quest.js)

Progress: First Blood, world-clear badges (one per world), Elective Explorer
Mastery (tag-based): Confounder Catcher, VIF Vanquisher, Odds Whisperer, Calibration Captain, Residual Reader, Weight Watcher (survey), Hazard Handler, Imputation Inspector
Behaviour: Unaided (10 first-try, no hints), Pitfall Spotter (spot-the-error), Honest Estimator (well-calibrated confidence)
Growth: Baseline Set, Growth Mindset (post-test done), Big Gain (+20 points)
Community (Phase 6): Peer Reviewer, Mentor



5.4 Game modes, bosses and events
The site has three play modes (details in Site design §4–6):

Quests: the guided world-by-world path (briefing → levels → boss).
Case files: 15–25 minute branching investigations (e.g. “The salt study reviewer”, “The village anomaly”): read output, choose actions, defend choices; scored by rubric.
Arcade: short repeatable drills built from generators (Residual Reader, Interval Invaders, OR↔︎PR Converter, Spot the Pitfall …) so a skill can be rehearsed with fresh numbers each time.
Daily review: a spaced queue (Leitner boxes) of the skills that are due or fading.
Boss fights: each world ends with a multi-part scenario; failing is cheap, retrying free.
Seasonal events (optional): e.g. Thesis Month with double-XP review quests.



5.5 Social, optional and safe
Cohort leaderboards are opt-in and off by default for residents; show relative growth, not just totals; team quests (pair review of each other’s analysis plan). No public ranking of identifiable learners without consent.


5.6 Anti-gaming

Hashing is anti-peeking only. For anything that counts (certificates), use server-side checking with signed attempts (Phase 6).
Randomised option order; per-learner numeric seeds; item pools (several parallel versions of each item).
Rate-limited hints; “show answer” forfeits XP; first-try rule stops trial-and-error farming.
Analytics flag implausibly fast completions.



5.7 Inclusive game design
All feedback is colour-independent (icons and text); prefers-reduced-motion honoured; keyboard-operable everything; a “calm mode” with no streaks, toasts or ranks for learners who find gamification stressful.

6.1 Item types
