⬜ Phase 4


Code lab check (auto-graded R)
Applied skills
⬜ Phase 4


Multi-select (select all that apply)
Assumption checklists
⬜ Phase 3





6.2 Item-writing standards (hard rules, linted)

Never make the key the longest option; keep option lengths within ±25% and within a 2.5× overall ratio.
No “all/none/both of the above”; no absolute words (always, never, only, exactly) in distractors alone.
No function-recall questions (e.g. “which function does mutate?”, “which argument gives odds ratios?”). Ask what a result means, what to do, or compute something.
Answers must not appear in the stem, in a hint, or be implied by stem-key word overlap.
Key position is irrelevant: markup order is permuted at build time (so the source never lists the key first) and display order is shuffled at run time.
Every distractor is a real misconception from the world’s misconception log, not a throwaway.
Every item has: world, 1–3 skill tags, difficulty 1–3, an explanation that teaches, and 1–3 non-revealing hints.
Stems are self-contained, in a public-health context, and avoid trick wording or double negatives.
Numeric items use values away from rounding ties; state the rounding in the stem.
Explanations appear only after an attempt or an explicit Show answer.



6.3 Quality gates

lint_quizzes.R (workshop decks) and lint_bank.R (quest bank) must pass in CI: zero hard failures.
Peer review checklist for each new item (two reviewers: a content expert and a “naïve” learner).
Hash-parity tests between R and JS for every item type; Playwright tests for every interaction.



6.4 Pre-/post-testing

Two parallel forms (A/B), 12 items each, mapped to the same skill tags; difficulty-balanced.
Confidence rating per answer (Guess/Probably/Certain) → calibration feedback (“you were certain and wrong on 3 items”).
Output: skill-by-skill profile → recommended next worlds → post-test gain (percentage points and normalised gain).
Planned extension: Form C for a delayed (3-month) retention test.



6.5 Psychometrics (once ≥ 100 learners)

Item difficulty (p-value), discrimination (point-biserial), distractor analysis (is any distractor never chosen?), time-on-item.
Retire or rewrite items with discrimination < 0.15 or difficulty outside 0.2–0.9.
Differential item functioning by background (R vs no-R experience) to detect unfair items.
Mastery model: a skill is “mastered” after 3 correct first-try items across ≥ 2 sessions (spaced).

title: Dungeons & Dataframes — Roadmap
text:
7. Auto-graded R labs (the biggest build)

7.1 Options









Option
Pros
Cons
Verdict




learnr + gradethis (Shiny)
Mature, real R, hints/solutions built in
Needs a Shiny server or shinyapps.io
Good for cohort deployments


webR / Quarto-live
R in the browser, static hosting, offline
Some packages unavailable/heavy (check gtsummary, performance)
Optional later mode (Phase 5), after a package-compatibility spike


Local scripts + verifiable result codes (hybrid)
Real RStudio workflow, real packages, no server, works offline
Codes can be shared unless seeded per learner
Chosen for Phases 3–4





7.1b The hybrid design (chosen)
Learners work in their own R (RStudio/Posit Cloud) on the repo’s labs. A tiny helper package/script (rqlab) provides rq_start(seed), rq_check("task-3", obj) for instant local feedback, and rq_submit() which prints a short result code (task results hashed with the learner’s seed and a lab version). The learner pastes the code into the site; the site verifies it and awards XP. No server, works offline, and the per-learner seed makes codes non-transferable. Details: Site design §6.


7.2 Pipeline (reuses what exists)

Solution scripts remain the single source of truth (#@ markers define blanks).
A grader generator produces testthat/gradethis checks per task: object exists, class/formula correct, estimate within tolerance, output text pattern.
Tiered hints per task (concept → structure → near-answer), each costing XP.
Tolerance policy: numeric checks use relative tolerance (e.g. 1%); string checks normalise case and whitespace; accept equivalent formulas (y ~ x1 + x2 ≡ y ~ x2 + x1).
Seeded variants: the learner seed regenerates the dataset, and checks compute expected values from the same seed.
CI runs every solution through the grader to prove solution ⇒ all checks pass and blank lab ⇒ checks fail.



7.3 Fairness and safety
Sandboxed execution only (webR runs in the browser); time limits; no network; clear, non-punitive error messages (“your model has the right outcome but the wrong predictor”).

title: World 1 · The Outcome Detective
text:
Briefing

Regression describes how the average of an outcome changes with one or more predictors, in real units. The first decision in any analysis is not the software; it is what type of outcome you have.











Outcome → model family: continuous → linear · binary → logistic · count → Poisson / negative binomial · ordered categories → ordinal logistic · unordered categories → multinomial · time-to-event → Cox · clustered or repeated → mixed models / GEE.


Correlation vs regression. Correlation is symmetric and unit-free; regression gives a directional slope in outcome units and can adjust for other variables.


cor(ncd$sbp, ncd$salt_g, use = "complete.obs")

[1] 0.4489003

coef(lm(sbp ~ salt_g, data = ncd))

(Intercept)      salt_g 
 107.420160    3.389337 



Missing data. A model silently drops any row with a missing model variable (complete-case analysis), so check missingness before modelling.


ncd |> summarise(across(c(bmi, salt_g, education), ~ sum(is.na(.x))))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
    bmi salt_g education
  <int>  <int>     <int>
1    18     18        15

title: World 1 · The Outcome Detective
text:
Level 1 · Roles and types

In the model sbp ~ salt_g + age, which term plays the role of the outcome (dependent variable)?

The residual error of the line
Participant age in years (age)
Daily salt intake (salt_g)
Systolic pressure (sbp)



A district programme records how many antenatal visits each woman made (0, 1, 2, …). What type of outcome is this?

A count of events
A nominal category
A continuous measurement
A time-to-event outcome



Hypertension (yes/no) will be analysed with age, BMI and salt intake in a cross-sectional survey. Which starting point fits the flowchart?

Linear regression because BMI is continuous
Logistic regression for the binary outcome
Poisson regression because prevalence is a rate
Cox regression because age is recorded



Place of delivery is recorded as home, PHC, district hospital or private hospital. Which model family suits this outcome?

Negative binomial regression
Binary logistic regression
Ordinal logistic regression
Multinomial logistic model

title: World 1 · The Outcome Detective
text:
Level 2 · Reading output

cor(ncd$sbp, ncd$salt_g, use = "complete.obs")
#> [1] 0.449
What does this number tell you?

A moderate positive association, but no slope in mmHg per gram
Each extra gram of daily salt adds 0.449 mmHg to systolic pressure
Salt intake causes about 45% of all the hypertension in the sample
Salt intake explains 44.9% of the variation in systolic pressure



ncd has 600 rows. bmi is missing for 18 people and salt_g for a different 18 people (no overlap). How many people stay in a model that uses both?

title: World 1 · The Outcome Detective
text:
Level 3 · Workflow

Put a sensible first-pass analysis in order, from first to last:

Add covariates chosen from a causal diagram
Plot the outcome against the main exposure
Fit the crude model and read the slope in its units
Report estimates with CIs and units

title: World 1 · The Outcome Detective
text:
Boss · The Table 1 detective

Boss: flag every flawed sentence in this Table 1 write-up (cross-sectional survey, n = 600).

Hypertensive adults were older (median 55 vs 45 years) and ate more salt (median 8.6 vs 6.6 g/day).
Salt intake therefore causes hypertension.
About 3% of BMI values were missing, so models used complete cases.
The Table 1 p-values show age and salt stay associated with hypertension after adjusting for each other.
Residence showed no difference between groups, so it is unrelated to blood pressure in every respect.
Tobacco use was more common among the hypertensive group (39% vs 26%).

title: Regression Analysis
text:
Regression Diagnostics
A fitted model is only trustworthy once its assumptions have been checked.

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model)









# Residuals vs fitted, and a normal Q-Q check
qqnorm(residuals(model))
qqline(residuals(model), col = "red")








Watch for: non-random patterns in residuals-vs-fitted (non-linearity), points far off the Q-Q line (non-normal residuals), and high-leverage points in the residuals-vs-leverage panel.

title: Regression Analysis
text:
Logistic Regression
When the outcome is binary rather than continuous, use glm() with a binomial family instead of lm().

data$outcome <- sample(c("Improved", "Not Improved"), 100, replace = TRUE)
data$outcome_bin <- ifelse(data$outcome == "Improved", 1, 0)

model_log <- glm(outcome_bin ~ age + treatment, data = data, family = binomial)
summary(model_log)


Call:
glm(formula = outcome_bin ~ age + treatment, family = binomial, 
    data = data)
